anc-0048,anc,Eswatini ANC Guidelines,text,,,3.4 Point of care tests > Haemoglobin for monitoring anaemia .,24,24,anc:8626a4622d,anc:22832a321e,anc-0047,anc-0049,167,"### **Haemoglobin for monitoring anaemia .**
* Check for pallor at every contact and check hemoglobin at contact 1,3, and 6.
* Each pregnant woman must be asked about her HIV status and offered HIV testing services at the first contact if negative or of unknown status (refer to the National Integrated HIV guidelines).

* If the pregnant woman refuses the test or is not willing to disclose the result of previous test or no test results available, assess for signs suggesting severe or advanced HIV infection; Counsel on benefits of testing and knowing their status, safer sex including use of condoms and benefits of involving and testing the Partner.","Eswatini ANC Guidelines

- All pregnant women are to be tested for glycosuria and proteinuria at every scheduled contact using a urine dipstick

anc-0051,anc,Eswatini ANC Guidelines,text,,,3.5 Laboratory,25,25,anc:73e5eff713,anc:73e5eff713,anc-0050,anc-0052,169,"## **3.5 Laboratory:**
- Test for Asymptomatic bacteriuria (ASB)
- Collect a midstream urine specimen to check for ASB through a Gram stain or culture at the 1<sup>st</sup> contact visit and repeated at 26 weeks (contact 3).
- For management of ASB <u>see section 7.2 of this guideline</u>.
- Full blood count (FBC).
- Conduct FBC testing for diagnosing anaemia and this will guide on the course of action.
- Normal hemoglobin level should be >11 g/dl
- If HB is <11 g/dl see section 7.1 for management
- On each subsequent contact look for conjunctival pallor; palmar pallor. Ifpallor is moderate or severe Check haemoglobin level(see section 7.1 of this guideline)","Eswatini ANC Guidelines

anc-0058,anc,Eswatini ANC Guidelines,text,,,3.7 Counselling and information provision > 3.7.1 Caffeine intake,28,28,anc:10ee0e49cf,anc:a9dda9842f,anc-0057,anc-0059,128,"### 3.7.1 Caffeine intake
- Women must be informed that a high daily intake (>300mg per day) is probably associated with a higher risk of low birth weight and pregnancy loss.
Explain that a cup of coffee contains about 60mg of caffeine whilst caffeine containing teas contain 50mg per 250ml cup.

anc-0067,anc,Eswatini ANC Guidelines,text,,,3.7 Counselling and information provision > 3.7.9 Baby stimulation,30,30,anc:236423866f,anc:a9dda9842f,anc-0066,anc-0068,291,"## 3.7.9 Baby stimulation
- Advise the pregnant woman on baby stimulation whilst in utero. The following are suggestions:
- Make contact with your baby in some way every day in a private, peaceful and quiet place (Be consistent)

- Get comfortable and relax - “tune out” from the rest of the world and focus only on your baby for at least 15 minutes twice a day or 30 minutes in one go. Soften your tight muscles by being calm and be slow whilst doing abdominal breathing which will settle you and your baby very quickly

- You can play music, simply talk to your baby or read the baby a story while you massage your belly and make this a habit and continue to do this throughout pregnancy, especially after the sixth month. Do gentle intentional touch with a purpose using small amount of simple baby oil, tissue oil or a cold pressed oil, so as to reduce the friction on the skin, and enable your hands to glide around the abdomen.

- Encourage the woman to allow the father to experiment with different ways of massaging the mother's belly as his touch will make her feel loved and special and these feelings will pass on to the baby who will feel the same.","Eswatini ANC Guidelines

anc-0073,anc,Eswatini ANC Guidelines,text,,,5.1 Weight gain,32,32,anc:a141cd9f29,anc:a141cd9f29,anc-0072,anc-0074,313,"## 5.1 Weight gain

Obesity during pregnancy increases the odds of spontaneous and recurrent miscarriages, suboptimal ultrasound screening for foetal anomalies, congenital heart and neural tube defects, wound Infections, anaesthesia complications, depression, breastfeeding problems, and many other adverse outcomes.

Most normal gestational weight gain occurs after 20 weeks of gestation. On an average a pregnant mother needs to gain 10-12 kg weight. However, recommended weight gain depends on the woman's pre-pregnant body mass index (BMI). Women who are underweight at the start of pregnancy (BMI < 18.5 kg/m2) should aim to gain 12.5–18 kg. Women who are normal weight at the start of pregnancy (BMI 18.5–24.9 kg/m2) should aim to gain 11.5–16 kg. Overweight women (BMI 25–29.9 kg/m2) should aim to gain 7–11.5 kg. Obese women (BMI > 30 kg/m2) should aim to gain 5–9 kg. Pregnant women are discouraged from engaging in stringent weight reduction diets. Nonetheless, women should be advised on appropriate weight management before pregnancy. If, however they are already obese by the time they get pregnant, nutrition counselling / advice should be provided to ensure optimum weight gain without compromising the maternal and foetal health status.","Eswatini ANC Guidelines

anc-0075,anc,Eswatini ANC Guidelines,text,,,5.3 Basics on Food Preparation,33,33,anc:d456ff3ab1,anc:d456ff3ab1,anc-0074,anc-0076,190,"## 5.3 Basics on Food Preparation

anc-0077,anc,Eswatini ANC Guidelines,text,,,5.5 Micronutrient supplementation,34,34,anc:3405bce9df,anc:3405bce9df,anc-0076,anc-0078,226,"## 5.5 Micronutrient supplementation

All pregnant women should take daily oral iron and folic supplementation with 30mg to 60 mg of elemental iron and 400 ug (0.4mg) folic acid to prevent anaemia, puerperal sepsis, low birth weight, and preterm birth.
Pregnant women should also receive daily calcium supplements of 1.5gram per day.
Encourage women to increase iron-intake by combining foods that help absorption such as spinach, livers, guavas and oranges with your vegetables.

Use margarine (sparingly) where possible as this is fortified with iron. The expecting mother to be encouraged to eat Folic acid rich foods such as green leafy vegetables, beans, bread and Calcium rich foods such as milk, yoghurt and cheese.

**NB:** The use of multiple micronutrient supplementation including multivitamins, Vitamin D, E, B6, Zinc, omega 3 & 6, etc. is not recommended for routine antenatal care clients.","Eswatini ANC Guidelines

anc-0078,anc,Eswatini ANC Guidelines,text,,,5.6 Key messages,34,34,anc:90d5aca827,anc:90d5aca827,anc-0077,anc-0079,158,"## 5.6 Key messages
- All pregnant women should be counseled on nutrition and diet at each ANC visit. These messages should be reinforced by the CHWs during home visits.

Management of the different complications is as follows:
### **6.1 Vaginal bleeding in early pregnancy**
Vaginal bleeding in early pregnancy may be associated with abortion; Ectopic pregnancy or Gestational trophoblastic disease (Molar pregnancy).

### *6.3.1 Definition*

Antepartum haemorrhage (APH) is bleeding from or into the genital tract, occurring from 28 weeks of pregnancy until before delivery of the baby. **NOTE: ANY BLEEDING IN A PREGNANT WOMAN SHOULD BE TAKEN SERIOUSLY.**
APH may be classified as:
* Spotting—staining, streaking, blood spotting on underwear or sanitary pad.
* Minor hemorrhage—blood loss less than 50 ml that has settled.
* Major hemorrhage—blood loss of 50-1000 ml with no signs of clinical shock
* Massive hemorrhage—blood loss greater than 1000 ml and/or signs of clinical shock."

* At first contact with pregnant woman, conduct a rapid blood test for syphilis(RPR)

anc-0109,anc,Eswatini ANC Guidelines,text,,,9.2 Data management,47,47,anc:bf34df1df9,anc:bf34df1df9,anc-0108,anc-0110,223,"## 9.2 Data management

Good Data Management is essential for the effective use of the information resources. All service providers must fully collect ANC related data for reporting on the ANC activities through the HMIS and CMIS. The data needs to be analyzed and presented by facility and regions to inform progress at all levels. Higher level indicator data should be collected through population based national surveys at intervals that agreed upon from time to time. e.g MMR, ANC coverage (at least once by skilled health personnel, and at least four times by any provider). column1: WHO physical activity recommendations by age group (children, adults, older adults, pregnant and postpartum women).

Children & adolescents (5-17 years): Recommendations: At least 60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous intensity PA daily. Include vigorous-intensity aerobic activities at least 3 days/week. Include muscle- and bone-strengthening activities at least 3 days/week.

Adults (18-64 years): Recommendations: At least 150-300 minutes of moderate-intensity PA per week, OR at least 75-150 minutes of vigorous-intensity PA per week, OR an equivalent combination of moderate and vigorous activity. Muscle-strengthening activities involving major muscle groups on 2 or more days per week.

Older adults (≥65 years): Recommendations: Same as adults (150-300 min moderate or 75-150 min vigorous). Muscle-strengthening activities 2 or more days per week. Multicomponent PA emphasizing functional balance and strength training 3 or more days/week to prevent falls.

Note: some activity is better than none. Inactive individuals should start with small amounts and gradually increase frequency, intensity, and duration. ncdimh-fig-smoking-cessation-p1,ncdimh,"Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)",diagram,ncdimh-fig-smoking-cessation,1/2,"Chapter 1: Prevention, Health Education and Routine Health Examinations > Nicotine Use > Smoking cessation approach",19,19,ncdimh:ccbf1fe896,ncdimh:bbccc17981,ncdimh-0034,ncdimh-0039,474,"### Smoking cessation approach in clinical practice (flowchart, with nicotine dependence table)

All smokers should be identified and their readiness to quit evaluated. If resistance to quitting exists, information and suitable follow-up should be provided. If the person is ready to make a quit attempt, evaluation of nicotine dependence, co-morbid and psychosocial factors should guide the choice of effective interventions.
1. Ask: do you smoke? do you know the risks? have you thought of quitting?
2. Alert: do you know the benefits of quitting? do you know that we can help you?
3. Assess: are you ready to quit?
4. Assist/arrange:
- No or maybe: give a motivational pamphlet and encourage follow-up; return to Ask at the next visit.
- Yes: arrange for cessation intervention.
5. Specific nicotine dependence review: Fagerstrom/CO levels; current smoking and history of quit attempts; social stressors/household smokers.
Dependence level (already attempted to quit / cigarettes per day / time to first cigarette after waking):
- Very high: yes / >30 / >5 min (printed)
- High: yes / 20-30 / 5-30 min
- Medium: yes / 10-20 / 30-60 min
- Low: no / <10 / >60 min
6. By dependence:
- Motivated, low dependence: could manage with counselling/support alone or NRT; support group, text/internet/smartphone-based support.

- Motivated, high dependence: probably will need added pharmacological support; assess medical/psychiatric history; evaluate capacity to purchase medicine; review availability of medication. Medication options: nicotine replacement therapy (patch/gum/spray), varenicline, bupropion.
7. Set quit date: arrange appropriate support and medication if needed.
8. Follow-up: assess withdrawal symptoms and drug side-effects; evaluate mood and psychosocial stressors; identify potential for relapse.
CO = carbon monoxide; NRT = nicotine replacement therapy.","Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)

ncdimh-fig-smoking-cessation-p2,ncdimh,"Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)",diagram,ncdimh-fig-smoking-cessation,2/2,"Chapter 1: Prevention, Health Education and Routine Health Examinations > Nicotine Use > Smoking cessation approach",19,19,ncdimh:ccbf1fe896,ncdimh:bbccc17981,ncdimh-0034,ncdimh-0039,474,"### Smoking cessation approach in clinical practice (flowchart, with nicotine dependence table)

All smokers should be identified and their readiness to quit evaluated. If resistance to quitting exists, information and suitable follow-up should be provided. If the person is ready to make a quit attempt, evaluation of nicotine dependence, co-morbid and psychosocial factors should guide the choice of effective interventions.
1. Ask: do you smoke? do you know the risks? have you thought of quitting?
2. Alert: do you know the benefits of quitting? do you know that we can help you?
3. Assess: are you ready to quit?
4. Assist/arrange:
- No or maybe: give a motivational pamphlet and encourage follow-up; return to Ask at the next visit.
- Yes: arrange for cessation intervention.
5. Specific nicotine dependence review: Fagerstrom/CO levels; current smoking and history of quit attempts; social stressors/household smokers.
Dependence level (already attempted to quit / cigarettes per day / time to first cigarette after waking):
- Very high: yes / >30 / >5 min (printed)
- High: yes / 20-30 / 5-30 min
- Medium: yes / 10-20 / 30-60 min
- Low: no / <10 / >60 min
6. By dependence:
- Motivated, low dependence: could manage with counselling/support alone or NRT; support group, text/internet/smartphone-based support.

- Motivated, high dependence: probably will need added pharmacological support; assess medical/psychiatric history; evaluate capacity to purchase medicine; review availability of medication. Medication options: nicotine replacement therapy (patch/gum/spray), varenicline, bupropion.
7. Set quit date: arrange appropriate support and medication if needed.
8. Follow-up: assess withdrawal symptoms and drug side-effects; evaluate mood and psychosocial stressors; identify potential for relapse.
CO = carbon monoxide; NRT = nicotine replacement therapy.","Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)

- Recognize triggers: stress, social pressure, certain places, emotions
- Use the '4 Ds': Delay, Distract, Deep breathing, Drink water
- Call a supportive friend or family member
- Remember health benefits: better sleep, more energy, improved health, saving money
## When to Refer
**Refer to **specialized alcohol treatment services** if:**
- AUDIT score ≥20 (likely alcohol dependence)
- Failed previous attempts to quit despite brief intervention
- Signs of withdrawal symptoms (tremors, sweating, anxiety, seizures)
- Co-occurring mental health disorders (depression, anxiety, psychosis)
- Severe alcohol-related medical complications (cirrhosis, pancreatitis)
- Patient requests specialized help","Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)

Unhealthy dietary patterns contribute significantly to non-communicable diseases in Eswatini. All clients >18 years attending a health facility should be screened for diabetes using the known risk factors below.
- No risk factors: re-evaluate.
- Risk factors present: test (HbA1c, fasting plasma glucose, oral glucose tolerance test, or random glucose):
- HbA1c <5.7% / FPG <100 mg/dl: encourage healthy lifestyle maintenance; retest at least annually.
- HbA1c 5.6-6.4% / FPG 100-125 mg/dl / OGTT 140-199 mg/dl: encourage lifestyle modification and retest every 6-12 months.
- HbA1c ≥ 6.5% / FPG ≥ 126 mg/dl: retest with a different test, and refer for treatment if still positive.

*Known risk factors for diabetes: physical inactivity; family history of diabetes; high-risk race or ethnicity (African, Indian); hypertension (≥ 140/90); HDL-C <35 or triglyceride > 250 mg/dL; history of gestational diabetes or gave birth to a baby ≥4.5 kg; history of heart disease; conditions associated with insulin resistance; polycystic ovary syndrome; malnutrition.

Adapted from the American Diabetes Association Standards of Medical Care in Diabetes. N.B.: the Ministry of Health recommends measuring glycaemia yearly in adults ≥ 18 years of age.","Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)

Obtain fasting lipids at baseline and annually. Then three parallel assessments, then treat to the target:
1. Calculate and categorize CV risk using the Framingham risk score (mdcalc.com - Framingham Risk Score). Risk categories: low risk < 10%; moderate risk 10%-19%; high risk > 20%.

- LDL-C: optimal <100 mg/dL; near or above optimal 100-129 mg/dL; borderline high 130-159 mg/dL; high 160-189 mg/dL; very high ≥190 mg/dL.
- Total cholesterol: desirable <200 mg/dL; borderline high 200-239 mg/dL; high ≥240 mg/dL.
- Triglycerides: normal <150 mg/dL; borderline high ≥150-199 mg/dL; high 200-499 mg/dL; very high ≥500 mg/dL.

ncdimh-fig-ckd-clinical-protocol,ncdimh,"Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)",diagram,ncdimh-fig-ckd-clinical-protocol,1/1,"Chapter 1: Prevention, Health Education and Routine Health Examinations > Routine Health Examinations > Chronic Kidney Disease > CKD clinical protocol (kidney health check)",29,29,ncdimh:1e27e695be,ncdimh:fa2b3aa589,ncdimh-fig-lipid-management,ncdimh-tbl-ckd-staging-heatmap,262,"### Chronic kidney disease clinical protocol: kidney health check, confirmation and staging

Offer a kidney health check to people with: diabetes; hypertension; established CVD; family history of kidney failure; obesity (BMI ≥30); current or past smoker/vaper; history of AKI aged ≥60 years; high index of suspicion in clients, especially paediatrics, with oedema and recurrent puffiness.
Tests: uACR, eGFR, and trace protein on urine dipstick.
- uACR ≥3 mg/mmol (yes): repeat uACR within 3 months. If uACR normal, complete a third test (preferably first morning void). CKD if a minimum of two uACRs ≥3 mg/mmol over 3 months.

- eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73m2 (yes): repeat eGFR within 7 days; if ≥20% reduction in eGFR, possible AKI: discuss with nephrologist. Repeat eGFR within 3 months. CKD if a minimum of two eGFRs <60 mL/min/1.73m2 over 3 months.
- No to both: repeat kidney health check (annually if aged ≥18, people with diabetes or hypertension).

If either (and/or) criterion is met: stage CKD with the staging table, using eGFR and uACR results.","Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)

ncdimh-fig-ckd-screening,ncdimh,"Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)",diagram,ncdimh-fig-ckd-screening,1/1,"Chapter 1: Prevention, Health Education and Routine Health Examinations > Routine Health Examinations > Chronic Kidney Disease > Algorithm for CKD screening",30,30,ncdimh:d66a3d1320,ncdimh:fa2b3aa589,ncdimh-tbl-ckd-staging-heatmap,ncdimh-tbl-diabetes-definition-classification,222,"### Algorithm for chronic kidney disease (CKD) screening
Target population:
- No markers of risk: do not screen.
- Risk factors (high blood pressure, diabetes, cardiovascular diseases, family history, HIV): screen.
Screen: test (urine dipstick, blood glucose, blood pressure, family history) and measure kidney function (serum creatinine; estimate the eGFR).
Determine if test results indicate CKD (eGFR <60 ml/min/1.73m2 or presence of albuminuria):
- No: rescreen based on the risks.

- Yes: lifestyle modification (smoking cessation; balanced diet; regular exercise; limit salt intake to <2 g/day); medical treatment (diabetes, BP and lipid control: SGLT2, ACEI/ARB, statins, metformin...); considerations (drug dosing; use of contrast media; CKD complications: anaemia, hyperkalaemia, bone disease, CVD...).
Then: retesting; follow-up visits; referral to nephrology when appropriate.","Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)

column3: Diabetes mellitus is a chronic metabolic condition in which the pancreas no longer produces enough insulin (impaired insulin secretion) or cells stop responding to the insulin that is produced (insulin resistance), resulting in increased blood glucose.

1. Type 1 diabetes: due to autoimmune b-cell destruction, usually leading to absolute insulin deficiency, including latent autoimmune diabetes of adulthood. 2. Type 2 diabetes: due to a progressive loss of b-cell insulin secretion, frequently on the background of insulin resistance.

Monogenic diabetes syndromes (neonatal diabetes; maturity-onset diabetes of the young). Diseases of the exocrine pancreas (such as cystic fibrosis and pancreatitis). Drug- or chemical-induced diabetes: glucocorticoid use, treatment of HIV/AIDS, or after organ transplantation. Gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM): diabetes diagnosed in the second or third trimester of pregnancy that was not clearly overt diabetes before gestation.
HbA1c <7% for most adults. HbA1c <6.5% for type 1 diabetes without hypoglycaemia. HbA1c <8% for people with frequent hypoglycaemia, limited life expectancy, or cardiovascular complications.
All clients on treatment should aim for a glycaemia (random or fasting) ranging 5-10 mmol/L.

ncdimh-fig-t2dm-pharmacological-treatment-p1,ncdimh,"Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)",diagram,ncdimh-fig-t2dm-pharmacological-treatment,1/2,Chapter 2: Endocrinology > Management of Type 2 Diabetes in Outpatient > Type 2 diabetes pharmacological treatment,34,34,ncdimh:2654452a76,ncdimh:9ebfac1d5c,ncdimh-tbl-diabetes-baseline-follow-up-checklist-p3,ncdimh-tbl-oral-glucose-lowering-agents-p1,481,"### Type 2 diabetes pharmacological treatment (flowchart, by HbA1c)
Newly diagnosed type 2 DM patient: check HbA1c. Health promotion for all (disease, medication adherence, nutrition, behaviour), individual and group.
By HbA1c at diagnosis:
- HbA1c <7%: lifestyle modification; recheck HbA1c in 6 months.
- HbA1c 7-8% (printed '<7%-8%'): start metformin [note 1]: 1. 500 mg OD; 2. recheck HbA1c in 3 months; 3. increase dose every 3 months until at goal or maximum tolerated dose.

- HbA1c 8-9.9% (printed '<8%-9.9%'): consider dual therapy: 1. start metformin 500 mg OD and titrate every 2 weeks to a maximum of 2 g if tolerated; 2. add a second drug (sulfonylurea, DPP-4 inhibitor, pioglitazone, GLP-1 agonists or SGLT-2 inhibitors).

- HbA1c >10%: consider insulin: consider starting the patient on insulin therapy alone or in combination with metformin (consult physician). Start at low-dose insulin and increase until target reached.
Follow-up after lifestyle modification or metformin:
- HbA1c <7%: 1. continue current medication; 2. recheck HbA1c in 6 months; 3. fasting blood glucose every 3 months.

- HbA1c >7%: 1. add a second OGLA, e.g. sulfonylurea, DPP-4 inhibitor, pioglitazone, GLP-1 agonists or SGLT-2 inhibitors; 2. recheck HbA1c in 3 months; 3. increase the dose of the second agent until glycaemic target reached, or maximum dose. If HbA1c remains >8%, review with physician and consider referral to the diabetes clinic for insulin management.
T2DM diagnosis criteria: 1. FPG > 7.0 mmol/L; 2. random glucose > 11.1 mmol/L; 3. need two positive tests, one must be FBG.
For older patients, it is reasonable to set the HbA1c goal at < 8%.

[note 1] Caution: metformin use in patients with reduced kidney function: 1. do not start new patients on metformin if CrCl < 45 ml/min; 2. continue metformin if already on it and CrCl is 30-45 ml/min, but repeat CrCl in 6 months; 3. stop metformin if CrCl < 30 ml/min.","Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)

ncdimh-fig-insulin-initiation-t2dm-p1,ncdimh,"Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)",diagram,ncdimh-fig-insulin-initiation-t2dm,1/2,Chapter 2: Endocrinology > Insulin Therapy in Type 2 Diabetes > Stepwise approach to insulin initiation in type 2 DM,38,38,ncdimh:8980469d4a,ncdimh:ba14ce9ea3,ncdimh-tbl-insulin-indications-t2dm,ncdimh-tbl-premixed-insulin-adjustment,625,"### Stepwise approach to insulin initiation in type 2 DM (flowchart)
Steps run from 1 injection (more flexible, lower patient complexity) to 3+ injections (less flexible, high complexity).
Step 1 - Basal insulin (usually with metformin), 1 injection:
Start: 10 units per day, or 0.1 to 0.2 units per kg per day.
Adjust: 10% to 15%, or 2 to 4 units, once or twice weekly to reach fasting BG target.
For hypoglycaemia: determine and address cause; decrease dose by 4 units or 10% to 20%.

If not controlled after fasting BG target is reached (or if dose > 0.5 units per kg per day), treat postprandial glucose excursions with mealtime insulin (consider an initial glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor agonist trial). Two options (2 injections, moderate complexity):
Option A - Add 1 rapid-acting insulin injection before the largest meal:
Start: 4 units, 0.1 units per kg, or 10% of basal dose; if A1C <8%, consider decreasing basal insulin by the same amount.
Adjust: increase dose by 1 to 2 units or 10% to 15% once or twice weekly until SMBG target is reached.
For hypoglycaemia: determine and address cause; decrease dose by 2 to 4 units or 10% to 20%.
If not controlled: consider basal-bolus (Step 3).
Option B - Change to premixed insulin twice daily:
Start: divide current basal dose into 2/3 a.m. and 1/3 p.m., or into 1/2 a.m. and 1/2 p.m.
Adjust: increase dose by 1 to 2 units or 10% to 15% once or twice weekly until SMBG target is reached.
For hypoglycaemia: determine and address cause; decrease dose by 2 to 4 units or 10% to 20%.
If not controlled: consider basal-bolus (Step 3).
Step 3 - Add 2 or more rapid-acting insulin injections before the largest meals (basal-bolus, 3+ injections, high complexity):
Start: 4 units, 0.1 units per kg, or 10% of basal dose per meal; if A1C < 8%, consider decreasing basal dose by the same amount.
Adjust: increase dose by 1 to 2 units or 10% to 15% once or twice weekly until SMBG target is reached.

column1: Stepwise approach to insulin initiation in type 2 DM (flowchart) (part 1 of 2).
Steps run from 1 injection (more flexible, lower patient complexity) to 3+ injections (less flexible, high complexity).
Step 1 - Basal insulin (usually with metformin), 1 injection:
Start: 10 units per day, or 0.1 to 0.2 units per kg per day.
Adjust: 10% to 15%, or 2 to 4 units, once or twice weekly to reach fasting BG target.
For hypoglycaemia: determine and address cause; decrease dose by 4 units or 10% to 20%.

Adjust: increase dose by 1 to 2 units or 10% to 15% once or twice weekly until SMBG target is reached.

If not controlled: consider basal-bolus (Step 3).

Start: divide current basal dose into 2/3 a.m. and 1/3 p.m., or into 1/2 a.m. and 1/2 p.m.
Adjust: increase dose by 1 to 2 units or 10% to 15% once or twice weekly until SMBG target is reached.
For hypoglycaemia: determine and address cause; decrease dose by 2 to 4 units or 10% to 20%.
If not controlled: consider basal-bolus (Step 3)."

Three stages, shown as three boxes:
1. Symptoms (loss of weight, polyuria, polydipsia, ...): increased risk of diabetes. Suspect diabetes.

ncdimh-0112,ncdimh,"Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)",text,,,Chapter 2: Endocrinology > Insulin Injection Technique > How to Inject Insulin with a Syringe,43,43,ncdimh:402efd6a0e,ncdimh:f195daf8ee,ncdimh-tbl-insulin-types-action,ncdimh-0113,354,"## **How to inject insulin with a Syringe**

ncdimh-fig-dka-algorithm-p1,ncdimh,"Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)",diagram,ncdimh-fig-dka-algorithm,1/2,Chapter 2: Endocrinology > Diabetic Emergencies > Algorithm for DKA,50,50,ncdimh:9eb1b4b0fb,ncdimh:5440a21ed1,ncdimh-tbl-dka-hhs-discharge,ncdimh-0140,676,"### Algorithm for DKA (flowchart: assessment, resuscitation, IV therapy, insulin, monitoring, cerebral oedema)
Immediate assessment:
- Clinical history: polyuria, polydipsia, nocturia, enuresis, weight loss, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, weakness, fatigue, confusion, level of consciousness.
- Clinical signs: dehydration; deep sighing respiration (Kussmaul); smell of ketones; lethargy/drowsiness.
- Biochemical features & investigations: ketones in urine; blood glucose; acidaemia (vpH < 7.3, HCO3 <15 mmol/L); urea, electrolytes; other investigations as indicated.
Diagnosis confirmed: diabetic ketoacidosis. Contact senior staff.
Then by clinical state:

A. Shock (reduced peripheral pulses), reduced conscious level/coma: resuscitation: airway ± NG tube; breathing (100% oxygen); circulation: 0.9% saline 10-20 ml/kg over 1-2 h, repeat until circulation is restored (see CE management). Then IV therapy (as B).

B. Dehydration >5%, not in shock, acidotic (hyperventilation), vomiting: IV therapy: saline 0.9% 10 ml/kg over 1 h, may repeat; calculate fluid requirements; correct fluid deficit over 24-48 hours; ECG for abnormal T-waves; add KCl 40 mmol per litre of fluid.
C. Minimal dehydration, tolerating oral fluid: therapy: start with SC insulin; continue oral hydration. If no improvement: IV therapy (as B).
After IV therapy: continuous insulin infusion at 0.05-0.1 unit/kg/hour, starting 1 hour after fluids initiated.
Critical observations: hourly blood glucose; hourly fluid input & output; neurological status at least hourly; electrolytes 2-hourly after starting IV fluid therapy; monitor ECG for T-wave changes.
Then:
- Acidosis not improving: re-evaluate IV fluid calculations, insulin delivery system & dose, need for additional resuscitation; consider sepsis.

- Blood glucose ≤17 mmol/L (300 mg/dL) or blood glucose falls >5 mmol/L/hour (90 mg/dL): IV therapy: change to 0.45% or 0.9% saline; add glucose to fluids (5%-12.5%) to prevent hypoglycaemia; adjust sodium infusion to promote an increase in measured serum sodium. When improved (clinically well, ketoacidosis resolved, tolerating oral fluids): transition to SC insulin: start SC insulin, then stop IV insulin after an appropriate interval.

- Neurological deterioration: warning signs: severe or progressive headache, slowing heart rate, irritability, confusion, decreased consciousness, incontinence, specific neurological signs. Exclude hypoglycaemia; is it cerebral oedema? CE (cerebral oedema) management: give mannitol 0.5-1 g/kg or 3% hypertonic saline; adjust IV fluids to maintain normal BP but avoid over-hydration; call senior staff; move to ICU; consider cranial imaging only after the patient is stabilized.","Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)

ncdimh-0140,ncdimh,"Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)",text,,,Chapter 2: Endocrinology > Hypoglycaemia,51,51,ncdimh:fcd5b58062,ncdimh:4da5cf338b,ncdimh-fig-dka-algorithm-p2,ncdimh-tbl-hypoglycaemia-symptoms,176,"## **Hypoglycemia**

Hypoglycemia is a medical emergency and should be treated promptly if serious complications are to be avoided. It is characterized by blood glucose levels <4 mmol/L. Some patients might experience hypoglycemic symptoms at higher blood glucose levels and clinicians should individualize care.
### **Common Causes**
* Increased physical activity without adjustment in food or insulin
* Delay or omission of meals/snacks

## Hypoglycemia

Hypoglycemia is a medical emergency and should be treated promptly if serious complications are to be avoided. It is characterized by blood glucose levels <4 mmol/L. Some patients might experience hypoglycemic symptoms at higher blood glucose levels and clinicians should individualize care.
### Common Causes
* Increased physical activity without adjustment in food or insulin
* Delay or omission of meals/snacks
* Poor injection technique
* Insulin overdose
* Inadequate carbohydrate intake
* Excessive alcohol use
* Sulphonylurea overdose
* Use of long-acting oral glucose-lowering agents
* Herbal medications causing liver failure when combined with diabetes drugs (timbita)"

Medications: Instruction: Discontinue all previous antihyperglycemic agents (injection/oral): yes/no; if yes, continue to calculate the insulin dose. Calculate the initial total daily insulin (TDI) per day: 0.25 units per kg: chronic kidney disease not on dialysis; 0.3 units per kg: underweight (BMI < 18.5), older age (≥65 years), haemodialysis; 0.4 units per kg: normal weight (BMI 18.5-24.9); 0.5 units per kg: overweight (BMI 25.0-29.9); ≥ 0.6 units per kg: obese (BMI ≥30), glucocorticoids, insulin resistance.

Basal insulin (longer acting): Instruction: Order 50% of the TDI. Should be given even if NPO*. Reduce dose by 25% if NPO*/poor intake/glycaemia well controlled. ___ units subcutaneous at ___ (Q24 or Q12 hours).

Bolus insulin (shorter acting): Instruction: Order 50% of the TDI. HOLD if NPO*, TPN**, low oral intake. Divided equally before each meal/bolus feed. If continuous feed: every 4 hours (rapid insulin), every 6 hours (regular insulin). Insulin REGULAR: ___ units SC 30 minutes BEFORE each meal/bolus feed, or every 6 hours if continuous feed.

Correction / sliding scale (shorter acting): Instruction: SHOULD be ordered and given even if NPO*. Eating patients: before meals and at bedtime (prefer rapid acting insulin); insulin REGULAR SC 30 minutes before meals. Bolus feed patients: before each feeding. TPN**, NPO* or continuous tube feeding: every 4 hours (rapid acting insulin), every 6 hours (regular insulin)."

ncdimh-0157,ncdimh,"Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)",text,,,Chapter 2: Endocrinology > Management of Comorbidities and Complications,56,56,ncdimh:be3f977bc5,ncdimh:4da5cf338b,ncdimh-tbl-diabetes-microvascular-complications-p3,ncdimh-0158,135,"## Management of Comorbidities and Complications
- Hypertension: target BP: if >130/80, Treat with ACEI (e.g., captopril) or ARB (e.g., losartan)
- Retinopathy: refer to ophthalmologist
- Nephropathy: if persistent proteinuria, start ACEI and refer to an Internist/Nephrologist
- Neuropathy: do foot exam at every visit

column1: Diabetes in pregnancy vs gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM): definition, onset, diagnostic criteria, management and postpartum follow-up (part 1 of 2).

Definition: Diabetes in pregnancy: Pregnancy in a woman known to have pre-existing diabetes (type 1 or type 2), or hyperglycaemia first detected in pregnancy that meets WHO criteria for diabetes in the non-pregnant state; Gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM): Hyperglycaemia first detected during pregnancy (usually in 2nd or 3rd trimester) that does not meet WHO criteria for diabetes in the non-pregnant state.
Timing of onset: Diabetes in pregnancy: May occur at any time, including the 1st trimester; Gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM): Typically develops in the 2nd or 3rd trimester.
Underlying type: Diabetes in pregnancy: Usually type 1 or type 2 diabetes mellitus; Gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM): Pregnancy-induced glucose intolerance.

Diagnostic criteria (WHO / IADPSG): Diabetes in pregnancy: Fasting plasma glucose (FPG) ≥ 7.0 mmol/L OR 2-hour OGTT (75 g glucose) ≥ 11.1 mmol/L OR random plasma glucose ≥ 11.1 mmol/L with symptoms; Gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM): Any one of the following (on 75 g OGTT): fasting ≥ 5.1 mmol/L; 1-hour ≥ 10.0 mmol/L; 2-hour ≥ 8.5 mmol/L.

Management focus: Diabetes in pregnancy: (not stated; see postpartum row for pre-existing diabetes care); Gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM): Dietary modification and physical activity. Monitor blood glucose regularly and start metformin if glycaemic control is not reached. Insulin therapy if lifestyle and metformin measures fail. Postpartum screening for type 2 DM."

ncdimh-0178,ncdimh,"Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)",text,,,Chapter 2: Endocrinology > Diabetes in Special Populations > Diabetes and TB,63,63,ncdimh:3d49d528d0,ncdimh:1dc9c38406,ncdimh-tbl-antidiabetic-arv-interactions-p2,ncdimh-tbl-dka-special-populations,106,"# **Diabetes and TB**

ncdimh-tbl-dka-special-populations,ncdimh,"Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)",table,ncdimh-tbl-dka-special-populations,1/1,Chapter 2: Endocrinology > Diabetes in Special Populations > Diabetic emergencies in special populations,63,63,ncdimh:76e4eace53,ncdimh:1dc9c38406,ncdimh-0178,ncdimh-0180,444,"### Diabetic emergencies (DKA/HHS) in special populations: HIV/TB co-infection, resource-limited settings, pregnancy, elderly

Diabetes and TB: anti-TB drugs can influence the metabolism of anti-diabetic medications. Rifampicin induces cytochrome P450 and increases the metabolism of most oral hypoglycaemic agents, which may worsen hyperglycaemia. Isoniazid inhibits cytochrome P450 and prolongs the effect of oral anti-diabetic drugs. Bedaquiline is also an enzyme inducer and reduces the effect of antidiabetic drugs.

column3: Screen for HIV if status unknown (rapid test on admission). Immune reconstitution can unmask T1DM. ARVs (especially older PI-based) can cause insulin resistance. Opportunistic infections (PCP, cryptococcal, TB) are common DKA precipitants. Maintain ARTs during crisis; liaise with HIV team.

No blood ketones: use urine ketones (≥2+ = significant). No VBG: treat on clinical picture + glucose + ketones. No syringe pump: 50 units in 500 ml NS (0.1 unit/ml) + drip control. No 0.45% NaCl: use 0.9% NaCl throughout with closer monitoring. Validate POC glucose meters for high glucose ranges >30 mmol/L.

DKA can occur at lower glucose (euglycaemic DKA in pregnancy). Involve obstetric team immediately. Fetal monitoring from 24 weeks onwards. Higher insulin requirements: do not underdose. Avoid bicarbonate unless pH <7.0.

Reduced physiological reserve: higher risk of fluid overload. More gradual fluid replacement over 48-72 hours. Increased thromboembolic risk: early LMWH prophylaxis. Exclude silent MI, stroke, UTI, pneumonia as precipitant. Assess cognition, falls risk, social support before discharge.

column1: Classification of osteoporosis by bone mineral density (BMD) T-score.
Normal: Criteria: BMD or BMC value (measured with DXA at either the spine, total hip or femur neck) within 1 SD of the young adult reference mean (T-score* at or above -1.0).
Low bone mass: Criteria: BMD or BMC value more than 1 SD but less than 2.5 SD below the young adult mean (osteopenia; T-score between -1.0 and -2.5).
Osteoporosis: Criteria: BMD or BMC value 2.5 SD or more below the young adult mean.
Severe osteoporosis: Criteria: BMD or BMC value more than 2.5 SD below the young adult mean, plus one or more fragility fractures.

These criteria were updated in 2008 and differ from those proposed by the WHO in 1994 by specifying a single reference site (the femoral neck) to measure BMD, providing a young normal reference range for women and men (the NHANES III reference data for femoral neck measurements in women aged 20-29 years), and by accommodating diagnostic criteria for men. *When standard deviation (SD) units are used in relation to the young healthy adult population, this is referred to as the T-score."

ncdimh-0194,ncdimh,"Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)",text,,,Chapter 2: Endocrinology > Diagnosis of Osteoporosis > Algorithm for the Assessment of Patients with Osteoporosis,70,71,ncdimh:6962314cbc,ncdimh:8a2a6937ce,ncdimh-fig-osteoporosis-assessment,ncdimh-tbl-osteoporosis-pharmacological-p1,293,"## Algorithm for the Assessment of Patients with Osteoporosis
**Clinical Risk Factors:**
* Advanced age
* Prior fracture
* Family History
* Excessive learners
* Diet/alcohol/smoking
* Fall propensity
* Secondary osteoporoses
## **Non-Pharmacological Management of Osteoporosis**
Postmenopausal women, and men age ≥50 years, with osteoporosis or who are at risk of fragility fracture are recommended:
1. A healthy, nutrient-rich balanced diet
2. An adequate intake of calcium (minimum 700mg daily) preferably achieved through dietary intake or otherwise by supplementation
3. To consume Vitamin D from foods be prescribed Vitamin D supplements of at least 800IU/day if they have identified Vitamin D insufficiency or risk factors for Vitamin D insufficiency.
4. A combination of regular weight-bearing and muscle strengthening exercise, tailored according to the individual patient’s needs and ability.
5. Advice about smoking and alcohol cessation

6. A falls assessment should be undertaken in all patients with osteoporosis and fragility fractures; those at risk should be offered exercise programmes to improve balance and/or that contain a combined exercise protocol","Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)

Hypothyroidism results from thyroid hormone deficiency most commonly due to iodine deficiency.

## **Management of Hypothyroidism**
- TSH level persistently >10mU/L; treat all patients due to, increased likelihood of progression to overt disease and a higher risk of congestive heart failure, cardiovascular disease and mortality.

- TSH levels (4.5–10mU/L); consider, treatment in patients younger than 65 with increased cardiovascular risk (e.g., previous cardiovascular disease, hypertension, documented diastolic dysfunction, atherosclerotic risk factors (dyslipidaemia, diabetes mellitus, smoker), goitre, positive antithyroid peroxidase antibodies, evidence of autoimmune thyroiditis by ultrasound, pregnancy, or infertility), particularly when TSH level is persistently >7mU/L.
- Levothyroxine therapy could be considered also for symptomatic middle-aged patients for a short period of time. If a clear beneficial effect is observed, levothyroxine therapy could be maintained.

- Persistently mildly increased TSH levels (>4.5-10mU/L) with positive Thyroid Antibody and thyroid sonographic findings typical of autoimmune thyroiditis.","Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)

ncdimh-0202,ncdimh,"Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)",text,,,Chapter 2: Endocrinology > Management of Hypothyroidism > Complications & Emergencies (Myxoedema Coma),74,74,ncdimh:5543b95d2a,ncdimh:9e326d80b0,ncdimh-0201,ncdimh-0203,252,"## **Complications & Emergencies associated with Hypothyroidism Myxedema coma – profound hypothyroidism**
**Clinical Presentation:** hypothermia, hypotension, hypoventilation, changes in mental status (coma rare), hyponatremia, hypoglycemia
**Medical history:** often precipitated by infection or major cardiopulmonary or neurologic illness
**Management principles:** supportive care is most important. Slow metabolism of drugs can lead to coma. Correction of hypothyroidism takes time.
- Load 5-8 mcg/kg T4 IV, then 50-100 mcg IV daily
- May also give 5-10 mcg T3 IV q8h if unstable with bradycardia and/or hypothermia (T3 more arrhythmogenic)
**Where IV is not available, give:**

- Liothyronine, Oral (crushed via NGT). Initially 10-20 mcg, depending on the patient's condition, with subsequent doses determined by the response (average 20 mcg q8h with close clinical and biochemical monitoring until there is sustained improvement).
- Maintain oral thyroxine alone, after an overlap period of a few days.","Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)

## Hyperthyroidism
Definition(s) and Classification of Hyperthyroidism
Hyperthyroidism is a set of disorders that involve excess synthesis and secretion of thyroid hormones by the thyroid gland, which leads to the hypermetabolic condition of thyrotoxicosis
- **Diffuse toxic goiter/Graves' disease** – autoimmune disorder with TSH-receptor stimulating Abs, is the most common form and accounts for more than 60% of cases
- **Thyroiditis** – thyrotoxic phase of subacute/granulomatous or painless/lymphocytic. Which is due to a temporary excess release of thyroid hormone
- **Toxic Multinodular Goiter/Plummer Disease** – occurs more commonly in the elderly with longstanding goiter
- **Toxic adenoma** – caused by a single hyperfunctioning follicular thyroid adenoma from a benign monoclonal tumor that usually is > 2.5cm diameter

- **Other aetiologies:** Genetic, infection, excessive iodine uptake, drugs (like amiodarone), hCG- secreting tumors (choriocarcinoma), gestation, and metastatic follicular thyroid carcinoma.","Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)

ncdimh-fig-primary-hyperthyroidism-diagnosis,ncdimh,"Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)",diagram,ncdimh-fig-primary-hyperthyroidism-diagnosis,1/1,Chapter 2: Endocrinology > Thyroid Disorders > Hyperthyroidism > Diagnostic algorithm for primary hyperthyroidism,78,78,ncdimh:65d3ded543,ncdimh:8fb4f4809f,ncdimh-0212,ncdimh-0215,109,"### Diagnostic algorithm for primary hyperthyroidism (by radioactive iodine uptake)
Primary hyperthyroidism: ↓ TSH, ↑ free T4, ↑ total T3. Next: radioactive iodine uptake (RAIU).
- Diffuse uptake: homogeneous: Graves' disease; heterogeneous: toxic multinodular goitre.
- Focal uptake: functioning adenoma.

- No uptake: measure serum thyroglobulin: low (↓): thyrotoxicosis factitia; high (↑): thyroiditis, iodine load, or struma ovarii.","Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)

ncdimh-fig-thyroid-storm-management,ncdimh,"Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)",diagram,ncdimh-fig-thyroid-storm-management,1/1,Chapter 2: Endocrinology > Thyroid Disorders > Hyperthyroidism > Management of thyroid storm > Recognition and management (flowchart),82,82,ncdimh:6140e1768a,ncdimh:a6e3c9e1ce,ncdimh-tbl-burch-wartofsky-score,ncdimh-tbl-thyroid-storm-treatment,217,"### Thyroid storm: recognition and management (flowchart)
1. Suspect thyroid storm (BWPS ≥45).
2. Identify precipitant(s).
3. Initial stabilization (ABC). Propylthiouracil (PTU) or methimazole.
4. Block thyroid hormone synthesis (≥ 1 h after ATD): Lugol's iodine 8 drops PO q6-8h, or NaI IV 0.25-0.5 g q6h.
5. Block peripheral effects: propranolol 60-80 mg OG 6-hourly, or 1 mg IV q10min (max 3); hydrocortisone 100 mg IV q8h.
6. Continuous monitoring & support: ECG, vitals, fluid balance, electrolytes. Adjust therapy as needed.

In addition to general supportive measures, therapy should be directed at the thyroid gland and the hypermetabolism and tachycardia. Patients should be monitored in an intensive or high care setting. The underlying precipitant should be actively treated and managed. Prevention is key: correct thyroid function before elective surgery.","Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)

ncdimh-0226,ncdimh,"Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)",text,,,Chapter 2: Endocrinology > Hyperthyroidism in Pregnancy > Introduction,83,83,ncdimh:fe26de1dca,ncdimh:c7fc879d71,ncdimh-tbl-thyroid-storm-treatment,ncdimh-0227,277,"## Introduction

A disease characterized by increased functional activity of the thyroid gland and increased secretion of thyroid hormones; It causes an increase in basal metabolism and other alterations at the systemic level occurring during pregnancy.
## Signs and Symptoms
Signs and symptoms are the same with the following additional symptoms:
- Difficulty gaining weight
- Intrauterine growth retardation (especially if associated with hypertensive disorders)
- Increased risk of miscarriage
- Premature birth
- Hyperemesis gravidarum
TSH-receptor antibodies are increased in pregnancy and the effects on the mother are typical of Graves' disease (exophthalmos, myxedema and goiter).
TSH-receptor antibodies cross the blood-placental barrier, binding to the fetal thyroid, producing fetal hyperthyroidism (regardless of maternal thyroid status).
The expression of this antibody is associated with:
- Fetal arrhythmia
- Hydrops Fetalis
- Malformations: alteration of the ossification nuclei and craniosynostosis.
- Stillbirth.
- Intrauterine growth restriction.
- ""Norm inserted"" placental abruption.","Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)

ncdimh-fig-hyperthyroidism-pregnancy,ncdimh,"Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)",diagram,ncdimh-fig-hyperthyroidism-pregnancy,1/1,Chapter 2: Endocrinology > Thyroid Disorders > Hyperthyroidism in Pregnancy > Management of hyperthyroidism in pregnancy,85,85,ncdimh:83fe2372e2,ncdimh:ca39daf28c,ncdimh-0229,ncdimh-0232,295,"### Management of hyperthyroidism in pregnancy (flowchart)
Two entry points:

- Known hyperthyroidism on ATD and wishing to conceive/pregnant: switch to a 'dose titration' regimen if on 'block and replace'. Use PTU pre-conception and in the 1st trimester; use CBZ (carbimazole) thereafter.
- New diagnosis of hyperthyroidism during pregnancy: commence anti-thyroid medication: PTU in the first trimester, CBZ thereafter.
Both: refer to endocrine physician. Then two parallel tracks:
Track 1 - check TFTs every 4 weeks (and LFTs every 4 weeks if on PTU):
- Free T4 above normal reference range: increase dose of ATD.
- Free T4 at or just above upper end of normal reference range: continue on current dose of ATD.
- Free T4 below upper end of normal reference range: decrease dose of ATD.
Repeat the 4-weekly checks throughout pregnancy. TFTs to be checked 6-8 weeks post-partum (printed 'at first ante-natal check').
Track 2 - check TRAb at 22 weeks and 36 weeks. If TRAb > 2-3 times the upper limit of normal: obstetric ultrasound for monitoring for fetal thyrotoxicosis.

Reference: Girling JC. Thyroid disease in pregnancy. The Obstetrician and Gynaecologist 2008; 10:237-243.","Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)

A long strip of at least 10 minutes will be made.

c. Search for signs of fetal goiter: week 22-24 and week 30-34.
2. Fetal heart rate evaluation for fetal tachycardia or arrhythmias, from week 28 onwards (request one per week).
A long strip of at least 10 minutes will be made.

Hyperthyroidism, Graves Disease
Description

Hyperthyroidism is a pathological syndrome in which tissue is exposed to excessive amounts of circulating thyroid hormones. The most common cause is Grave's disease, although thyroiditis may also present with thyrotoxicosis.
Diagnostic Criteria
Clinical
- Poor school performance
- Weight loss
- Tremor
- Palpitations
- Proptosis
- Heat intolerance
- Fatigue
- Warm moist hands"

**Cushing's Syndrome**

Cushing syndrome is a clinical condition resulting from prolonged exposure to excessive glucocorticoids from either endogenous or exogenous sources. The most common cause of Cushing's syndrome is from the administration of exogenous sources.

ncdimh-0235,ncdimh,"Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)",text,,,Chapter 2: Endocrinology > Cushing's Syndrome > Common Presenting Symptoms,88,89,ncdimh:d18716cb74,ncdimh:a64577648e,ncdimh-0234,ncdimh-0239,280,"## Common presenting symptoms include

- Weakness of the proximal muscles
- Easily bruises and striae
- Hirsutism

## Diagnosis of Cushing's Syndrome
At least two first-line tests should be abnormal to establish the diagnosis of Cushing's syndrome
- The low-dose dexamethasone suppression tests
- 24hrs urinary cortisol,
- Late night salivary cortisol
- Differential Diagnostic Testing to established, the cause of Cushing's syndrome
- ✓ Morning serum ACTH
- ✓ High dose dexamethasone suppression test

- Pituitary CT - sensitivity of about 50% for identifying microadenomas
- MRI pituitary sensitivity up to 100%
- Adrenal ultrasonography/CT for suspected Adrenal source
# Treatment of Cushing's syndrome
Without therapy, Cushing's syndrome is often fatal.
- Typically, due to CV, HTN or infectious complications.
- With therapy Symptoms improve over 2-12 months.
# Definitive Therapy
Surgery by source when possible
- Adrenal source - Adrenalectomy
- Pituitary source - Transphenoidal resection
- Ectopic source - Tumor Resection","Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)

A diagnosis of Hypertension is confirmed on the following criteria:

A systolic blood pressure [SBP] of 140 mmHg or more, or a diastolic blood pressure [DBP] of 90 mmHg or more. This must be measured on 2-3 separate visits within 4 weeks. A minimum of 3 BP readings at a minimum of 2 minutes apart must be taken at each visit.
**A single clinic blood pressure of ≥180/110 mmHg with evidence of cardiovascular disease confirms hypertension.**
**NB: If there is evidence of target organ damage without hypertension diagnosis, conduct investigations for other causes of target organ damage.**

**For those in whom hypertension is not diagnosed, monitor blood pressure readings annually. In all these patients reinforce a dietary approach to stop hypertension (DASH) diet and lifestyle modification.**
### **Patient Assessment**

At every visit, patients with hypertension should have a medical history taken, undergo a clinical examination and have blood and urine evaluation done as needed. Follow up management should be individualised.","Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)

ncdimh-0270,ncdimh,"Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)",text,,,Chapter 3: Cardiology > Hypertension > Resistant Hypertension,100,100,ncdimh:e506f2e41f,ncdimh:768318eae3,ncdimh-tbl-secondary-hypertension-p3,ncdimh-0271,327,"## Resistant Hypertension

- If seated office BP >140/90 mmHg in patients managed with three or more antihypertensive medications at optimal (or maximally tolerated) doses including a diuretic, first **exclude causes of pseudo-resistance** (poor BP measurement technique, white coat effect, nonadherence, and suboptimal choices in antihypertensive therapy), and substance-induced increases in BP.
- **Screen patients for secondary causes** as appropriate.

- **Optimize the current treatment regimen** including health behaviour change and diuretic-based treatment (maximally tolerated doses of diuretics, and optimal choice of diuretic: use of thiazide-like rather than thiazide diuretics, and initiation of loop diuretics for eGFR <30 ml/min/1.73m² or clinical volume overload).

- Add a low dose of spironolactone as the **4th line agent** in those whose serum potassium is <4.5 mmol/L and whose eGFR is >45 ml/min/1.73m² to achieve BP targets. If spironolactone is contraindicated or not tolerated, amiloride, doxazosin, eplerenone, clonidine, and beta-blockers are alternatives, or any available antihypertensive class not already in use.

- **REFER!!!!!!Resistant hypertension should be managed in specialist centres with sufficient expertise, and resources necessary to diagnose and treat this condition.**","Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)

ncdimh-0271,ncdimh,"Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)",text,,,Chapter 3: Cardiology > Hypertension > Hypertensive Emergencies > Definition,100,100,ncdimh:6faf392d44,ncdimh:ccb0c6eed2,ncdimh-0270,ncdimh-0272,231,"### Definition
**Hypertensive Emergency:** High blood pressure >180/120 plus end-organ damage:
- **Neurologic:** hypertensive encephalopathy, cerebral vascular accident/cerebral infarction, subarachnoid hemorrhage, intracranial hemorrhage
- **Cardiovascular:** myocardial ischemia/infarction, acute left ventricular dysfunction, acute pulmonary edema, aortic dissection, unstable angina pectoris
- **Other:** acute renal failure/insufficiency, retinopathy, eclampsia, microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia.
**Hypertensive urgency:** SBP > 180 OR DBP >120 without end-organ damage
- Nonadherence to previously prescribed antihypertensive medications is the most common factor leading to acute severe hypertension.
- Hypertensive emergencies is managed with intravenous medications guided by the type of target-organ damage.

- Hypertensive urgencies should be managed with oral medications and arrangements for prompt follow-up.","Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)

ncdimh-0294,ncdimh,"Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)",text,,,Chapter 3: Cardiology > Hypertension > Hypertension and Other Comorbidities,107,108,ncdimh:c93073098d,ncdimh:768318eae3,ncdimh-0293,ncdimh-fig-aspirin-primary-prevention,233,"## **Hypertension and Other Comorbidities**

* In addition to BP control, the therapeutic strategy should include lifestyle changes, body weight control and the effective treatment of the other risk factors to reduce the residual cardiovascular risk.
* Lifestyle changes are recommended in patients with Hypertension and other Comorbidities.
* LDL-cholesterol should be reduced according to risk profile:
(1) >50% and <70 mg/dL (1.8 mmol/L) in hypertension and CVD, CKD, DM or no CVD and high risk.
(2) >50% and <100 mg/dL (2.6 mmol/L) in high-risk patients.
(3) <115 mg/dL (3 mmol/L) in moderate-risk patients.

* Fasting serum glucose levels should be reduced below 126 mg/dL (7 mmol/L) or HbA1c below 7% (53 mmol/mol). s-UA should be maintained below 6.5 mg/dL (0.387 mmol/L), and <6 mg/dL (0.357 mmol/L) in patients with gout.
* Antiplatelet therapy should be considered in patients with CVD (secondary prevention only)","Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)

ncdimh-fig-aspirin-primary-prevention,ncdimh,"Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)",diagram,ncdimh-fig-aspirin-primary-prevention,1/1,Chapter 3: Cardiology > Hypertension > How to use Aspirin for CV Disease Primary Prevention,108,108,ncdimh:2893c0dddf,ncdimh:768318eae3,ncdimh-0294,ncdimh-0297,153,"### How to use aspirin for primary prevention of cardiovascular disease (decision flowchart)
Aspirin for primary prevention, by age:
- 60 years or above: don't start aspirin for primary prevention.
- 40-59 years: calculate the 10-year CV risk.
- Risk <10%: don't start aspirin for primary prevention.
- Risk >10%: share the decision with the individual, weighing:
- Benefits: 12% reduction in MI; 12% reduction in stroke.
- Risks: 58% increase in GI bleeding; 31% increase in hemorrhagic stroke; no impact on mortality; no impact on cancer.
- If agreed on starting: aspirin 81 mg; stop at age 75.","Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)

### **Treatment of Hypertension in Pregnancy**
## **Mild Hypertension**
Drug treatment is recommended at persistent BP >150/95 mm Hg in all pregnant women.

Drug treatment is recommended at persistent BP >140/90 mm Hg in gestational hypertension, preexisting hypertension with superimposed gestational hypertension; hypertension with subclinical HMOD at any time during pregnancy.
*First Choices:* methyldopa, beta-blockers (labetalol), and dihydropyridine-calcium channel blockers (DHP- CCBs) (nifedipine [not capsular], nicardipine).

ncdimh-0299,ncdimh,"Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)",text,,,Chapter 3: Cardiology > Hypertension > (a) Hypertension in Pregnancy > Treatment of Hypertension in Pregnancy > Severe Hypertension; Post-partum and Breastfeeding,109,110,ncdimh:d7625d270a,ncdimh:96afee454b,ncdimh-0298,ncdimh-0301,256,"## **Severe Hypertension**
At BP >170 mm Hg systolic and/or >110 mm Hg diastolic: immediate hospitalization is indicated (emergency).

Treatment with intravenous labetalol (alternative intravenous nicardipine, esmolol, hydralazine, urapidil), oral methyldopa or DHP-CCBs (nifedipine [not capsular] nicardipine). Add magnesium (hypertensive crisis to prevent eclampsia).
**In pulmonary oedema: Nitroglycerin intravenous infusion. Sodium-nitroprusside should be avoided due to the danger of foetal cyanide poisoning with prolonged treatment.**
**Delivery in gestational hypertension or pre-eclampsia:** At week 37 in asymptomatic women. Expedite delivery in women with visual disturbances, haemostatic disorders.
# **Blood Pressure Post-partum:** If hypertension persists, any of recommended drugs except methyldopa (postpartum depression).

**Breastfeeding:** All antihypertensives excreted into breast milk at low concentrations. Avoid atenolol, propranolol, nifedipine (high concentration in milk). Prefer long acting CCBs.","Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)

Hypertension remains a risk factor for cardiovascular morbidity and mortality in older patients, however the balance of benefits and harms when considering antihypertensive drugs in this group are often reported as unclear. - For patients aged 65 and above

- ✓ For those with isolated systolic hypertension the primary goal of treatment is to lower SBP in the 140 to 150 mmHg range. However, a reduction of office SBP in the 130 to 139 mmHg range may be considered if well tolerated, albeit cautiously if DBP is already below 70 mmHg.

- ✓ Office BP should be lowered to a SBP in the 140 to 150 mmHg range and to a DBP. However, reduction of office SBP between 130 to 139 mmHg may be considered if well tolerated, albeit cautiously if DBP is already below 70 mmHg.
- When starting treatment in older patients, drugs should be commenced at the lowest dose and titrated slowly as adverse effects increase with age.

- In older persons where treatment is being targeted to <120 mmHg systolic, close follow-up of patients is recommended to identify treatment-related adverse effects including hypotension, syncope, electrolyte abnormalities and acute kidney injury.
- Clinical judgement should be used to assess the benefit of treatment against the risk of adverse effects in all older patients with lower grades of hypertension.

ncdimh-0305,ncdimh,"Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)",text,,,Chapter 3: Cardiology > Hypertension > (c) Hypertension in Paediatric Population > Definition; Hypertensive Emergency and Urgency in Children,111,112,ncdimh:cc24532cbd,ncdimh:9183e91141,ncdimh-0304,ncdimh-0306,339,"## Note: Investigations should be based on etiology.

**Hypertension** is defined as systolic and/or diastolic blood pressure the 95th percentile for gender, age, and height percentile on at least three consecutive occasions. A sustained blood pressure of > 115/80 is abnormal in children between 6 weeks and 6 years of age. A sustained blood pressure of >130/90 mmHg in a child older than 13 years is defined as hypertension. Measure blood pressure with the child in a sitting or supine position with the entire arm in line with the level of the heart. **Severe hypertension suggests renal disease**.

**Hypertensive Emergency/Crisis** exists when CNS signs of hypertension appear, such as encephalopathy, convulsions, retinal haemorrhages or blindness. Great care is required to reduce the blood pressure in a controlled manner to avoid potentially serious consequences of impaired autoregulation of cerebral blood flow.

**Hypertensive urgency** is defined as a significant elevation of blood pressure without accompanying end- organ damage. Patients are generally symptomatic with complaints of headache, blurred vision and nausea, despite the lack of end-organ involvement.

ncdimh-0306,ncdimh,"Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)",text,,,Chapter 3: Cardiology > Hypertension > (c) Hypertension in Paediatric Population > How to measure BP in Paediatric Client; Categories of Hypertension,112,112,ncdimh:da468baa52,ncdimh:9183e91141,ncdimh-0305,ncdimh-tbl-paeds-secondary-htn-causes,217,"## **How to measure BP in Paediatric Client**
A valid assessment of the blood pressure is of extreme importance. The blood pressure is measured by standard auscultation technique in children >1 year of age.
Measure the BP in at least one limb, preferably the right upper arm. If hypertension is present, measure BP in all four limbs.

One should use the widest cuff that can be applied to the upper arm. The cuff bladder must encircle at least 80% of the upper arm and should cover at least 40% of the distance between the acromion and the olecranon.
### **Categories of Hypertension**
* Normal: below 90th percentile.
* Elevated Blood Pressure: 90th–95th percentile or BP >120/80 mmHg.
* Stage 1 Hypertension: >95th–99th percentile plus 12 mmHg.
\*\*\*In adolescents if BP >140/90 mmHg, even <95th percentile
* Stage 2 Hypertension: >99th percentile plus 5 mmHg.","Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)

ncdimh-0309,ncdimh,"Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)",text,,,Chapter 3: Cardiology > Hypertension > (c) Hypertension in Paediatric Population > Management,113,113,ncdimh:d8d07f66b8,ncdimh:9183e91141,ncdimh-tbl-paeds-secondary-htn-causes,ncdimh-0310,167,"## **Management**
- Refer/Admit patient to pediatric high dependency unit
- Monitor BP every 60 minutes for 24 hours
- Insert peripheral line for drugs
- Bed rest
- Control fluid intake and output (restriction)
- Restrict dietary sodium
- Manage end organ effects
- Do not combine drugs of the same class
- Furosemide, IV, 1–2 mg/kg as a bolus slowly over 5 minutes
- If oliguric, maximum dose: 5 mg/kg/dose

- Nifedipine 0.25-0.5mg/kg (max: 10mg) sublingual. May be repeated 6 hours later, thereafter every 12 hours OR amlodipine, oral, 0.2 mg/kg/dose daily. OR Hydralazine 0.2-0.6mg/kg/dose. The dose can be repeated every 4 hours.
- Refer the patient to a specialist","Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)

ncdimh-0310,ncdimh,"Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)",text,,,Chapter 3: Cardiology > Hypertension > (c) Hypertension in Paediatric Population > Recommendations,113,113,ncdimh:0ca74b643b,ncdimh:9183e91141,ncdimh-0309,ncdimh-tbl-paeds-bp-95th-by-age,176,"## **Recommendations**
- For acute or chronic hypertension blood pressure needs to be lowered cautiously

# HEART FAILURE

Definition: Heart Failure is a clinical syndrome arising from the inability of the heart to generate enough cardiac output to meet metabolic demands or the ability to only do so on high filling pressure. It is characterized by typical symptoms (e.g. breathlessness, ankle and pedal oedema, and fatigue) that may be accompanied by signs (e.g. elevated jugular venous pressure, pulmonary crackles and peripheral oedema) caused by a structural and/or functional cardiac abnormality, resulting in a reduced cardiac output and/or elevated intracardiac pressures at rest or during stress."

NYHA classification - the stages of heart failure:
- Class I - no symptoms and no limitation in ordinary physical activity, e.g. Shortness of breath when walking, climbing stairs, etc.
- Class II - mild symptoms (mild shortness of breath and/or angina) and slight limitation during ordinary activity.
- Class III - marked limitation in activity due to symptoms, even during less-than-ordinary activity, e.g. Walking short distances (20-100 m), comfortable only at rest.
- Class IV - severe limitations. Experiences symptoms even while at rest. Mostly bedbound patients.
- No NYHA class listed or unable to determine.
HF is defined based on EF by HFrEF (EF≤40%), HFmrEF (EF41-49%), HFpEF(EF>50%).","Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)

ncdimh-fig-hf-diagnosis-management-p1,ncdimh,"Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)",diagram,ncdimh-fig-hf-diagnosis-management,1/2,Chapter 3: Cardiology > Heart Failure > Algorithm for Diagnosis and Management of Heart Failure,117,117,ncdimh:0e0291ddc4,ncdimh:89408ebdf0,ncdimh-tbl-ross-hf-children,ncdimh-fig-hf-preserved-ef,440,"### Algorithm for diagnosis and management of heart failure (by facility level, echo availability, congestion; guideline-directed therapy and CRT)
1. Suspected heart failure? Take a history and examine.

- Clinic history: symptoms (acute: raised JVD, PND, lower limb swelling); function limitation (NYHA class); prior cardiac disease, pregnancies; prior comorbidities (HTN, disease, others); drugs, toxins.
- Physical exam: vital signs; signs of congestion (raised JVD, hepatomegaly); lower limb swelling; murmur; crackles.
2. Investigations by facility level:
- Health Center: LABS: U&Es, CBC, glycemia, CXR, ECG. If congested with SatO2 <90%: give IV Lasix (furosemide) 40 mg and transfer to the regional hospital.
- Regional Hospital: U&Es, CBC, glycemia, HbA1c, chest X-ray, ECG, +/- cardiac ultrasound. Refer on to the referral hospital as needed.
- Referral Hospital: U&Es, CBC, glycemia, HbA1c, ferritin, chest X-ray, cardiac ultrasound, ECG, coronary CTA, cardiac MRI.
3. Still suspect heart failure? (at DH/PH/referral hospital) Yes → Is heart ultrasound (echo) available?
- No: treat as HFrEF (EF ≤40%) and refer to cardiology.
- Yes: HFrEF & HFmrEF on echo → look for cardiomyopathy or valvular heart disease.
- Not congested: work up causes (genetics, inflammatory, toxins, pregnancy, metabolic).
4. If congested (from either path): IV Lasix (8-hourly), morphine (if no low BP), nitrates (if available), oxygen (if low SpO2).
- Cardiogenic shock: IV inotropes/pressors, until euvolemic.
5. When euvolemic, start guideline-directed medical therapy: 1. RAASi; 2. beta-blocker; 3. MRA (EF ≤35%); 4. SGLT2i → RAASi + BB + MRA ± SGLT2i.
6. After 3 months of GDMT, if EF ≤35% plus LBBB: CRT (cardiac resynchronisation therapy).","Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)

ncdimh-fig-hf-preserved-ef,ncdimh,"Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)",diagram,ncdimh-fig-hf-preserved-ef,1/1,Chapter 3: Cardiology > Heart Failure > Algorithm for Diagnosis and Management of Heart Failure > Preserved ejection fraction,118,118,ncdimh:4925ef563d,ncdimh:0e0291ddc4,ncdimh-fig-hf-diagnosis-management-p2,ncdimh-fig-hf-other-causes-p1,202,"### Heart failure with LVEF >50%: hypertensive heart disease (HFpEF) and mitral stenosis (algorithm, continued)
Still suspect heart failure? (at HC/PH/referral hospital) → Heart ultrasound available? Yes → LVEF >50%:
- With BP >180/110 mmHg: hypertensive heart disease (HFpEF); calculate the H2FPEF score.
- If congested: IV Lasix (8-hourly), oxygen (if low SpO2), position semi-sitting.
- Screen for comorbidities: diabetes, dyslipidemia, AF, CAD, HTN.
- BP control: 1. SGLT2i; 2. beta-blocker (if AF); 3. RAASi; 4. CCB.
- With mitral restricted opening, hockey-stick deformity, dilated LA on echo, and an apical diastolic murmur: mitral stenosis.
- Causes: 1. rheumatic; 2. calcific; 3. congenital; 4. valvulitis.
- Treat: Lasix (if congested); penicillin V (rheumatic); beta-blocker (atenolol).","Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)

ncdimh-fig-hf-other-causes-p1,ncdimh,"Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)",diagram,ncdimh-fig-hf-other-causes,1/2,"Chapter 3: Cardiology > Heart Failure > Algorithm for Diagnosis and Management of Heart Failure > Valvular, right heart and pericardial disease",119,119,ncdimh:26759be230,ncdimh:0e0291ddc4,ncdimh-fig-hf-preserved-ef,ncdimh-tbl-decompensated-hf,422,"### Heart failure algorithm (continued): valvular heart disease, right heart failure, pericardial disease, other diagnoses and precipitants of acute heart failure; inotrope dosing
Still suspect heart failure? (at HC/PH/referral hospital) → Heart ultrasound available? Yes → LVEF >50%:
- BP normal or high, valvular heart disease & CHD: 1. Lasix (if overloaded); 2. RAASi (high BP or LV remodelling); 3. +/- penicillin V; 4. cardiology consult.
- If congested: IV Lasix (8-hourly), oxygen (if low SpO2), position semi-sitting.
- Dilated RV + D-shape sign, TAPSE <1.7 cm, loud P2: right heart failure. 1. Lasix (if congested); 2. screen for the cause of pulmonary HTN (acute/chronic lung disease, PE, other).

- Pericardial effusion: pericardial disease. 1. Pericardiocentesis (if tamponade): refer to cardiologist; 2. screen for and treat the cause: infections (TB, HIV, CMV, EBV), metabolic (thyroid disorders, uremia), malignancy, connective tissue disease; 3. others.
- Heart failure unlikely and normal heart ultrasound: consider other plausible diagnoses.

Precipitants of acute heart failure: 1. dietary indiscretion (alcohol, high salt); 2. medical non-adherence; 3. renal failure (acute/CKD progression); 4. new drugs (BB, CCB, NSAIDs, others); 5. arrhythmias, valve dysfunction; 6. new infection (pneumonia, others); 7. myocardial ischemia/infarction, PE; 8. metabolic (thyroid, DKA, pancreatitis); 9. hypertensive crisis.

Inotropes: IV dobutamine or dopamine 200 mg. Dose: 10-20 mcg/kg/min. Example for a 70 kg adult: 2 ampoules in 50 cc NS by syringe pump at 5.25-10.5 cc/h; or, if no syringe pump, 5 ampoules in 500 cc NS over 24 hours = 21 cc/h ≈ 7 drops/min. Keep MAP ≥ 65.","Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)

ncdimh-0339,ncdimh,"Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)",text,,,Chapter 3: Cardiology > Ischemic Heart Disease > Diagnosis > Clinical History of Angina,122,122,ncdimh:5c8609b74c,ncdimh:a495215136,ncdimh-0338,ncdimh-0340,208,"### **Clinical History of Angina:**

A detailed clinical history of angina includes assessing the magnitude, location, severity, duration, and precipitating factors of angina. The presence of a typical nature of the discomfort, precipitating factors and relieving factors should be suggestive of angina. Retrosternal chest pain, heaviness, pressure type with radiation to neck, jaw, epigastrium, shoulder, and left arm. Patients are usually asymptomatic at rest and chest pain is precipitated by exercise, cold weather, or emotional stress with a duration of 2 to 10 min and relieved by rest or taking sublingual nitrates. In addition to chest discomfort, dyspnoea, palpitations, syncope or fatigue may also be present and sometimes may be the only symptom. Physical examination is required to corroborate and strengthen the diagnosis.","Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)

ncdimh-fig-chest-pain-approach-p1,ncdimh,"Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)",diagram,ncdimh-fig-chest-pain-approach,1/2,Chapter 3: Cardiology > Ischemic Heart Disease > Approach to Patient with Chest Pain,124,124,ncdimh:a7a21bf7a0,ncdimh:f577a18fe3,ncdimh-tbl-ihd-management,ncdimh-0345,504,"### Approach to the patient with chest pain (flowchart: ACS, STEMI/NSTEMI/unstable angina, pericarditis, pneumothorax, pneumonia, aortic dissection, pulmonary embolism)
1. Initial assessment with vitals (BP, all peripheral pulses, RR, temperature, JVP, SpO2) and physical examination (CVS, respiratory system, GIS).
- Hemodynamically unstable: stabilize and immediately assess for STEMI, aortic dissection, massive pulmonary embolism, pericardial tamponade.
- Hemodynamically stable: evaluate the causes of chest pain.
2. Obtain a 12-lead ECG, echo and CXR (all patients).
3. ECG diagnostic or suggestive of ACS? YES → Does the patient have typical or atypical angina pattern, radiation, diaphoresis, cardiac risk factors?
- ST elevation → STEMI.
- ST depression and/or T wave inversion → check cardiac markers (troponin, CK-MB) at baseline and repeat at 6 hrs:
- Suggestive history, positive cardiac enzymes and ECG changes = NSTEMI.
- Cardiac markers negative, new onset, crescendo or rest angina = unstable angina.
- Pericarditis.
4. History and ECG suggestive of ACS? NO → X-ray chest or echo:
- X-ray chest: area of lucency in lung parenchyma and chest wall → pneumothorax; infiltrate (with history and labs consistent with infection) → pneumonia.
- Widened mediastinum (and history consistent with aortic dissection) and flap on echo → refer for dedicated imaging (CT aortogram): aortic dissection.
5. Assess risk for pulmonary embolism:
- Low risk: send D-dimer, X-ray evaluation. Elevated D-dimer, or echo showing dilated RA/RV or McConnell sign → high risk.
- High risk for pulmonary embolism (D-dimer elevated): refer for CT pulmonary angiogram to rule out PE.

6. If ECG, X-ray, cardiac markers and echo are normal: rule out other causes of chest pain based on history and available investigations. Patients with nonspecific chest pain, no ECG changes at presentation and at discharge from emergency, and normal cardiac enzymes can be discharged and followed up in OPD.","Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)

3. ECG diagnostic or suggestive of ACS? YES → Does the patient have typical or atypical angina pattern, radiation, diaphoresis, cardiac risk factors?
- ST elevation → STEMI.
- ST depression and/or T wave inversion → check cardiac markers (troponin, CK-MB) at baseline and repeat at 6 hrs:
- Suggestive history, positive cardiac enzymes and ECG changes = NSTEMI.
- Cardiac markers negative, new onset, crescendo or rest angina = unstable angina.
- Pericarditis.

- X-ray chest: area of lucency in lung parenchyma and chest wall → pneumothorax; infiltrate (with history and labs consistent with infection) → pneumonia.

A chart running from LOW to HIGH probability of myocardial infarction:
I. Clinical setting, symptoms and vital signs: from localised chest discomfort (low) to widespread pain (higher) to cardiac arrest needing CPR/shock (high).
II. ECG: normal ECG → mild ST depression → ST depression → ST elevation.
III. Troponin level at 0 h: − (low); −/+; +; ++; +++ (high).
IV. Troponin change within 1, 2 or 3 h: −; −/+; +; ++; at the highest level, if any of the above, consider direct rule-in.
Triage decision:
- Troponin − at 0 h and no change: rule out MI.
- Troponin −/+ or +: observe.
- Troponin ++ or more, or ST elevation: rule in MI.

ncdimh-0358,ncdimh,"Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)",text,,,Chapter 3: Cardiology > Stroke Management > Definition(s) and Classification of Stroke,130,130,ncdimh:18f13bc54b,ncdimh:ca2e70bdf1,ncdimh-tbl-fibrinolysis-contraindications,ncdimh-tbl-stroke-steps-1-2-p1,135,"### **Definition(s) and Classification of Stroke**
**Definition**
Stroke is the acute neurologic injury that results from brain vessel flow blockade either from ischemia or hemorrhage.
**Classification**
Stroke is classified into two major types and one minor type:
- Brain ischemia (80%) due to thrombosis, embolism, or systemic hypoperfusion.
- Brain hemorrhage (20%) due to intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) or subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH).

- Transient ischemic attack (TIA): temporary neurologic symptoms, which last less than 24 hours.","Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)
