ncdimh-fig-palliative-care-trajectory-levels,ncdimh,"Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)",diagram,ncdimh-fig-palliative-care-trajectory-levels,1/1,Chapter 11: Palliation > Palliative Care in the Trajectory of the Patient's Illness,291,291,ncdimh:5671fe7a4b,ncdimh:c96dac8dd5,ncdimh-tbl-opioids-in-ckd,ncdimh-0843,419,"### Palliative care across the illness trajectory, and palliative care tasks by level (referral hospital, regional hospital, health centre/primary clinic, home)

Trajectory (diagram): from presentation/diagnosis, therapies to modify disease (curative, restorative intent) decrease over time while therapies to relieve suffering and/or improve quality of life (palliative care) increase; palliative care continues through life closure and active dying to death, followed by bereavement care.
Palliative care by level:
- Referral hospitals: holistic assessment and reassessment; appropriate pain and symptom management; holistic care with specialised management (radiotherapy, chemotherapy, surgery).

- Regional hospitals: holistic assessment and reassessment; appropriate pain and symptom management; initiate or adjust the PC regimen for mild, moderate or severe symptoms; plan continued PC after discharge to a lower level or home; refer to referral hospitals for specialised management.

- Health centre/primary care clinic: visit the patient at home in the first week after discharge if possible; holistic pain assessment; pain and symptom management using the WHO ladder; emotional support; liaise with CHWs who visit patients at home; request oral morphine solution for PC patients in the HC catchment area; request advice from the regional hospital if needed; refer complicated cases to the regional hospital.

- Home: recognise and report inadequately relieved pain or other physical, psychological or social distress, and improper use of morphine or other medicines; provide emotional support; educate the family on daily care (feeding, hygiene, mobility, medications).","Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)

ncdimh-0843,ncdimh,"Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)",text,,,"Chapter 11: Palliation > Pain Management > Morphine: dose calculation, paediatric dose, side effects, naloxone",292,292,ncdimh:9857f254fc,ncdimh:ef4b6adba5,ncdimh-fig-palliative-care-trajectory-levels,ncdimh-tbl-adjuvant-analgesics,420,"## **How to calculate the dose of morphine PR:**

Add up all the morphine given in the past 24 hours. That gives the total dose required in 24 hours. Then divide by 2 to give the 12 hourly doses. E.g. morphine 10mg given every 4 hours = 6x10mg in 24 hours = 60mg in 24 hours = 30mg every 12 hours. The dose of morphine PR is 30mg twice daily.
Pediatric dose: 0.2 to 0.3 mg /kg (10-15mg) initial dose, 4hrly PO/SL and IV/SC 0.1mg/kg.
Side effects of morphine include are constipation, nausea, and vomiting, sedation, dry mouth, sweating, hallucinations, myoclonus, urinary retention, pruritus, hyperalgesia etc.
**Constipation is the most common side effect. The hand that writes opioids should also write laxatives.**
Morphine reduces gastrointestinal motility and secretion leading to constipation. A stimulant laxative like Bisacodyl, reduces the ring contraction and facilitate propulsive activity.
Sedation and nausea usually resolve after a few days. A patient will need to be reassured and given an antiemetic if they experience nausea.

Physical dependence may develop but drug addiction to morphine in patients with palliative care is very rare. Withdrawal symptoms when morphine is stopped or the dose is reduced are due to physical dependence.
Therefore the morphine dose should only be reduced slowly whilst the patient adjusts to coming off morphine.

**Respiratory depression is a very rare side effect in pain management when morphine is correctly titrated in palliative care. Naloxone is an antidote if respiratory depression develops. Dilute 400 micrograms (1amp) in 9ml normal saline and give 2.5ml (100 micrograms) IV every 1-2 minutes for titrating response**","Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)

ncdimh-box-tuning-fork-test,ncdimh,"Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)",text,ncdimh-box-tuning-fork-test,1/1,Chapter 12: Podiatry > Diabetic Foot > Screening > Tuning Fork Examination,297,297,ncdimh:3e6d0b72c6,ncdimh:fd76871779,ncdimh-0853,ncdimh-tbl-diabetic-foot-risk,168,"> **How to perform the 128 Hz tuning fork test for diabetic neuropathy**
> 1. Ask the patient to close his/her eyes.
> 2. Tap a 128 Hz tuning fork and place it on the patient's sternum to confirm vibration.
> 3. Tap the tuning fork and place it on a bony prominence of the foot (distal phalanx of the great toe).
> 4. Ask the patient to tell you when vibration is felt on the foot and when it stops.
> 5. If sensation is impaired, continue to assess more proximally (e.g. mid-dorsal foot, medial malleolus, mid-fibula, patella).
> 6. Repeat on the other leg.

> Note: any bony prominence of the foot can be tested, but the best point for the vibration test is the great toe.","Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)

column1: How to perform the 128 Hz tuning fork test for diabetic neuropathy.
1. Ask the patient to close his/her eyes.
2. Tap a 128 Hz tuning fork and place it on the patient's sternum to confirm vibration.
3. Tap the tuning fork and place it on a bony prominence of the foot (distal phalanx of the great toe).
4. Ask the patient to tell you when vibration is felt on the foot and when it stops.
5. If sensation is impaired, continue to assess more proximally (e.g. mid-dorsal foot, medial malleolus, mid-fibula, patella).
6. Repeat on the other leg.
Note: any bony prominence of the foot can be tested, but the best point for the vibration test is the great toe."

ncdimh-0861,ncdimh,"Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)",text,,,Chapter 12: Podiatry > Diabetic Foot > Importance of Off-Loading in DFU Management,300,300,ncdimh:87ec97ca31,ncdimh:72aafe8f92,ncdimh-fig-dfu-key-steps,ncdimh-tbl-dfu-offloading-p1,133,"## **Importance of Off-Loading in DFU Management**
* **Pressure Reduction:** Chronic pressure on ulcerated areas prevents the natural healing process, leading to further tissue damage, infection, and even amputation in severe cases.
* **Healing Promotion:** By off-loading the ulcerated site, the blood flow improves, inflammatory responses are regulated, and collagen formation is supported.

* **Infection Prevention:** Reduced pressure minimizes the risk of infection due to less friction and moisture retention at the wound site.","Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)

ncdimh-0865,ncdimh,"Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)",text,,,Chapter 12: Podiatry > Post-Amputation Management > Immediate Post-Operative Care,301,302,ncdimh:775104241d,ncdimh:af70c411da,ncdimh-0864,ncdimh-0866,416,"## **Post-Amputation Management of Patients**
<u>Key Components of Post-Amputation Care</u>
Post-amputation management includes a multidisciplinary approach involving the following key areas:
**Immediate Post-Operative Care**
**(a) Wound Care and Healing**
- **Criteria for Wound Monitoring:**
✓ Assess wound daily for signs of infection (e.g., redness, warmth, purulent drainage, and fever).
✓ Evaluate wound healing progress using tools like the Wound Healing Score (WHS), considering factors like wound size, exudate levels, and presence of infection.
✓ Non-healing or chronic wounds should be managed with advanced dressing materials (e.g., hydrocolloids, foam dressings) and, if needed, NPWT (Negative Pressure Wound Therapy).
**(b) Pain Management**
- **Pain Assessment Criteria:**
✓ Use standardized pain assessment scales such as the Visual Analog Scale (VAS) or McGill Pain Questionnaire.
✓ Early post-operative pain should be managed with opioids (short-term use) combined with NSAIDs (e.g., ibuprofen) for inflammation control.
✓ Phantom limb pain may be managed with medications like gabapentin, amitriptyline, or pregabalin.
✓ Ensure regular reassessment of pain intensity and adjust analgesia accordingly.
(c) **Infection Prevention**
- Antibiotic Therapy Criteria:
✓ Prophylactic antibiotics should be administered during the first 24-48 hours post-surgery, particularly in diabetic and immunocompromised patients.

✓ If infection is suspected, cultures should be taken from the wound bed, and broad-spectrum antibiotics (e.g., piperacillin-tazobactam or vancomycin) should be initiated until culture results guide de-escalation.","Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)

ncdimh-0866,ncdimh,"Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)",text,,,Chapter 12: Podiatry > Post-Amputation Management > Infection Prevention; Rehabilitation and Mobility Support,302,302,ncdimh:cd1fdc1d5d,ncdimh:af70c411da,ncdimh-0865,ncdimh-0867,240,"## <u>Rehabilitation and Mobility Support</u>
**(a) Early Mobilization and Physical Therapy**
- Criteria for Initiation:
✓ Early post-operative mobilization should begin within 48-72 hours to prevent complications such as deep vein thrombosis (DVT) and pneumonia.
✓ Initiate physical therapy (PT) with an emphasis on strengthening remaining muscles, improving balance, and preventing contractures.
**(b) **Prosthetic Fitting and Training****
- Criteria for Prosthesis Fitting:
✓ Prosthetic fitting should begin once the surgical wound has healed adequately (usually after 4-6 weeks, depending on the type of amputation).
✓ Consider the patient's physical activity level, lifestyle, and comorbid conditions in the choice of prosthetic.
✓ Prosthetic Training should be initiated after fitting, with a focus on ambulation, balance, and functional use.

✓ Prosthesis Maintenance: Ensure regular check-ups to monitor fit and function of the prosthesis.","Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)

ncdimh-0867,ncdimh,"Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)",text,,,Chapter 12: Podiatry > Post-Amputation Management > Long-Term Rehabilitation and Psychological Screening,302,302,ncdimh:502277736a,ncdimh:af70c411da,ncdimh-0866,ncdimh-0868,210,"## <u>Long-Term Rehabilitation</u>
**Criteria for Long-Term Rehabilitation:**
- Multidisciplinary teams should be involved in creating individualized rehabilitation plans.
- Set clear goals for mobility, independence, and reintegration into daily activities.
- Occupational therapy should also be included to assist with adaptations in daily living (e.g., use of assistive devices, home modifications).
**Psychological Screening Criteria:**
- Regular screening for depression, anxiety, and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) using validated tools like the PHQ-9 or HADS.
- Psychological support should be provided to help the patient cope with the emotional and mental impact of amputation.

- Referral to mental health professionals (e.g., psychologists, psychiatrists) should be made as needed for long-term psychological counselling.","Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)

ncdimh-fig-painful-diabetic-neuropathy,ncdimh,"Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)",diagram,ncdimh-fig-painful-diabetic-neuropathy,1/1,Chapter 12: Podiatry > Peripheral Neuropathy > Treatment of Neuropathic Pain in Diabetic Foot,305,305,ncdimh:4ff161085e,ncdimh:3d782552ba,ncdimh-tbl-peripheral-neuropathy-types,ncdimh-tbl-neuropathic-pain-drugs-p1,258,"### Treatment of painful diabetic neuropathy (flowchart): first-line anticonvulsants or antidepressants, second-line SNRIs, opioid-like drugs, topicals, third-line SSRIs and opioids
Patient presenting with painful neuropathy → rule out other causes of neuropathy → establish treatment goals → optimise glycaemic control.
- First-line therapy: anticonvulsants (pregabalin, gabapentin) or antidepressants (TCAs and SNRIs: amitriptyline, duloxetine).
- Second-line therapy: SNRIs (venlafaxine or desvenlafaxine); opioid-like drugs (tramadol or tapentadol ER); topical treatments (lidocaine 5% patch or capsaicin 0.075% cream).
- Third-line therapy: SSRIs (citalopram or paroxetine or escitalopram); opioids (oxycodone controlled release).

ER = extended release; SNRI = serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor; SSRI = selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor; TCA = tricyclic antidepressant. Adapted from Snyder MJ, Gibbs LM, Lindsay TJ. ncdimh-box-mdd-assessment-p1,ncdimh,"Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)",text,ncdimh-box-mdd-assessment,1/2,Chapter 13: Psychiatry > Major Depressive Disorder > Screening and Diagnosis of Major Depressive Disorder,308,308,ncdimh:49eeed1f75,ncdimh:85dc052829,ncdimh-0881,ncdimh-tbl-antidepressants-summary-p1,484,"> **Major depressive disorder: 8-step assessment, DSM-5/ICD-11 criteria (5 of 9 for 2+ weeks), severity classification and when to refer urgently**
> Assessment steps:
> 1. Screen: 'Have you felt sad/depressed most of the time for the past 2 weeks?' AND 'Have you lost interest in activities you usually enjoy?'
> 2. Assess core symptoms: 5 or more of 9 criteria present for 2+ weeks.
> 3. Assess functional impairment: work, relationships, self-care, daily activities.
> 4. RULE OUT: bipolar disorder (past mania?), psychosis, medical causes (hypothyroidism, anaemia, HIV, stroke, diabetes).
> 5. Screen for suicide/self-harm: 'Do you have thoughts of harming yourself or not wanting to live?'
> 6. Assess alcohol and substance use (may co-occur or cause symptoms).
> 7. Determine severity: mild / moderate / severe (any psychotic features?).
> 8. DIAGNOSIS confirmed if 5+ criteria are met, at least 1 being depressed mood or anhedonia.

> DSM-5 / ICD-11 criteria (5 of 9, lasting 2+ weeks): depressed mood most of the day (or irritability in children/adolescents); markedly diminished interest or pleasure (anhedonia); significant weight loss/gain or appetite change; insomnia or hypersomnia nearly every day; psychomotor agitation or retardation (observable by others); fatigue or loss of energy nearly every day; feelings of worthlessness or excessive/inappropriate guilt; difficulty concentrating or making decisions; recurrent thoughts of death or suicidal ideation.

> Severity: mild – few symptoms beyond the minimum, mild functional impairment; moderate – between mild and severe, moderate impairment; severe – most symptoms, marked impairment, may have psychotic features.

> When to refer urgently: active suicidal ideation with plan or intent; psychotic features (hallucinations, delusions); severe self-neglect or inability to care for self; no response after 2 adequate medication trials; suspected bipolar disorder.","Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)

ncdimh-box-suicide-risk-depression-follow-up,ncdimh,"Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)",text,ncdimh-box-suicide-risk-depression-follow-up,1/1,Chapter 13: Psychiatry > Major Depressive Disorder > Suicide Risk Assessment and Follow-up,310,310,ncdimh:683f1fc0ff,ncdimh:85dc052829,ncdimh-tbl-antidepressants-summary-p2,ncdimh-tbl-mdd-pharmacological-p1,365,"> **Depression: suicide risk assessment (mandatory), risk-level actions, follow-up schedule and PHQ-9 rescreening**

> SUICIDE RISK ASSESSMENT – mandatory in all depression cases. Ask directly: 'Are you having thoughts of harming yourself or ending your life?' If YES, assess: plan? method? intent? previous attempts? access to means (medications, weapons)?
> - HIGH RISK: hospitalise / urgent referral; remove access to lethal means immediately.
> - MEDIUM RISK: safety plan; close follow-up within 2-3 days; involve a trusted person/carer.
> - ALL risk levels: do not leave alone; mobilise social support; document the safety plan.
> FOLLOW-UP – depression (2 weeks initially, then monthly, then every 3 months):
> - Weeks 2-4: assess side effects and suicidal ideation (especially adolescents on SSRIs).
> - Weeks 4-6: has mood/interest improved? If no response, increase the dose or switch medication.
> - Weeks 8-12: full remission expected; reinforce adherence for the full course (9-12 months minimum).
> - After 9-12 months symptom-free: discuss gradual tapering over weeks to months.
> - 3+ recurrent episodes: consider long-term maintenance therapy.
> - Screen for re-emergence of symptoms at every follow-up after stopping treatment.

> PHQ-9 can be used for screening and follow-up: clients scoring 0-9 are rescreened every 6 months; those scoring 10 and above are reassessed 2 weeks after the initial visit and then at every follow-up visit.","Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)

column1: Depression: suicide risk assessment (mandatory), risk-level actions, follow-up schedule and PHQ-9 rescreening.

SUICIDE RISK ASSESSMENT – mandatory in all depression cases. Ask directly: 'Are you having thoughts of harming yourself or ending your life?' If YES, assess: plan? method? intent? previous attempts? access to means (medications, weapons)?
- HIGH RISK: hospitalise / urgent referral; remove access to lethal means immediately.
- MEDIUM RISK: safety plan; close follow-up within 2-3 days; involve a trusted person/carer.
- ALL risk levels: do not leave alone; mobilise social support; document the safety plan.
FOLLOW-UP – depression (2 weeks initially, then monthly, then every 3 months):
- Weeks 2-4: assess side effects and suicidal ideation (especially adolescents on SSRIs).
- Weeks 4-6: has mood/interest improved? If no response, increase the dose or switch medication.
- Weeks 8-12: full remission expected; reinforce adherence for the full course (9-12 months minimum).
- After 9-12 months symptom-free: discuss gradual tapering over weeks to months.
- 3+ recurrent episodes: consider long-term maintenance therapy.
- Screen for re-emergence of symptoms at every follow-up after stopping treatment.

PHQ-9 can be used for screening and follow-up: clients scoring 0-9 are rescreened every 6 months; those scoring 10 and above are reassessed 2 weeks after the initial visit and then at every follow-up visit."

ncdimh-0903,ncdimh,"Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)",text,,,"Chapter 13: Psychiatry > Substance Use Disorder > Definitions (intoxication, overdose)",313,314,ncdimh:03e588c7be,ncdimh:98080bcf59,ncdimh-0902,ncdimh-0905,399,"## <u>Substance Use Disorder</u>
## **Definition(s) and Classification**
- Is a psychiatric disorder classified under Substance Related and Addictive Disorders
- It begins at any age, mostly during adolescence.
**Acute intoxication** is a transient condition following intake of a psychoactive substance in disturbances of consciousness, cognition, perception, affect or behaviour.
**Overdose** is the use of any drug in such an amount that acute adverse physical or mental affects are produced.

**Withdrawal** is the experience of a set of unpleasant symptoms following the abrupt cessation or reduction in dose of a psychoactive substance; it has been consumed in high enough doses and for a long enough duration for the person to be physically or mentally dependent on it. Withdrawal symptoms are, essentially, opposite to those that are produced by the psychoactive substance itself.

**Harmful use** is a pattern of psychoactive substance use that damages health. This damage maybe physical, e.g. liver disease, or mental, e.g., episodes of depressive disorder. It is often associated with **social consequences** **e.g. family or work problems**.

**Dependence** is a cluster of physiological, behaviour and cognitive phenomena in which the use of a psychoactive substance takes on a much higher priority for a given individual than other behaviours that once had greater value. It is characterised by a strong craving to use the substance and a loss of control over its use. It is often associated with high levels of substance use and the presence of a withdrawal state upon cessation.","Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)

ncdimh-0905,ncdimh,"Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)",text,,,"Chapter 13: Psychiatry > Substance Use Disorder > Diagnostic Criteria (DSM-5, alcohol use disorder)",314,314,ncdimh:3326a305ca,ncdimh:98080bcf59,ncdimh-0903,ncdimh-0906,365,"## <u>Screening and Diagnosis</u>
- Screening is done using the Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test (AUDIT) tool.
## <u>Diagnostic Criteria:</u>
According to Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders Fifth Edition [DSM-V].

If a client/ patient presents with the problematic pattern of alcohol use leading to clinically significant impairment or distress, as manifested by at least two of the following, occurring within a 12-month period:
1. Alcohol is often taken in larger amounts or over a longer period than was intended.
2. There is a persistent desire or unsuccessful efforts to cut down or control alcohol use.
3. A great deal of time is spent in activities necessary to obtain alcohol, use it or recover from its effects.
4. Craving, or a strong desire or urge to use alcohol.
5. Recurrent alcohol use resulting in a failure to fulfill major role obligations at work, school, or home.
6. Continued alcohol use despite having persistent or recurrent social or interpersonal problems caused or exacerbated by the effects of alcohol.
7. Important social, occupational, or recreational activities are given up or reduced because of alcohol use.
8. Recurrent alcohol use in situations in which it is physically hazardous.
9. Alcohol use is continued despite knowledge of having a persistent or recurrent physical or psychological problem that is likely to have been caused or exacerbated by alcohol.
10. Tolerance
11. Withdrawal symptoms","Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)

ncdimh-0907,ncdimh,"Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)",text,,,Chapter 13: Psychiatry > Substance Use Disorder > Non-Pharmacological Management,315,316,ncdimh:4499ced89b,ncdimh:98080bcf59,ncdimh-0906,ncdimh-0908,405,"## Non-Pharmacological Management

(a) **Psychologically based treatment:** Psychologically based treatment for AUD is delivered in a specialty addiction treatment program. Clinicians should refer patients for psychological interventions, tailored dependent on individual needs, preferences, psychosocial factors, and available resources. Options for treating individuals with AUD include:
(i) Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT)
(ii) Motivational Interviewing (MI), and
(iii) Motivational Enhancement Therapy (MET)
These therapies may be provided as: Occupational therapy
AUD counselling or Psychotherapy with a Substance Use Disorder (SUD) counsellor, Clinical Psychologist OR
Short to long term rehabilitation
(b) **Mutual Support Programs:** Mutual support programs include AA and the 12-step facilitation interventions effective in increasing abstinence and improving alcohol-related outcomes.
(c) Provide advice on behaviour change whenever in contact with the patient.
(d) Encourage meaningful occupational engagement, constructive use of free time and leisure pursuits to decrease probability of relapses.
(e) Avoid people, places and activities that could potentially lead to relapse.
(f) Involve patient's family or caregiver in the management plan by providing information on the impact of drug use, especially the one used by the patient.
(g) Encourage patient to attend self-help support groups such as AA, NA for continuation of care to prevent relapses.

(h) Identify what will motivate them to change their addictive behaviour. Use these factors to help the person be motivated to change and keep going.","Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)

ncdimh-0909,ncdimh,"Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)",text,,,Chapter 13: Psychiatry > Substance Use Disorder > Alcohol Withdrawal Syndrome,316,316,ncdimh:9f766ec207,ncdimh:98080bcf59,ncdimh-0908,ncdimh-tbl-alcohol-withdrawal-sedative,232,"## Alcohol Withdrawal Syndrome  (red)

In individuals with AUD, an abrupt cessation or significant reduction of alcohol use can precipitate an acute alcohol withdrawal syndrome within 4 to 12 hours of last alcohol use. The syndrome presents with anxiety, agitation, tremor, and sympathetic nervous system activation. More severe outcomes present with seizure and delirium tremens, and if untreated may be fatal. Symptoms may persist for as long as 5 days.
Mild to moderate alcohol withdrawal syndrome can be managed in the outpatient primary care setting using benzodiazepines.

Use a validated screening tool for predicting the development of severe alcohol withdrawal such as the Prediction of Alcohol Withdrawal Severity Scale (PAWSS). A PAWSS score of < 4 is considered low risk for complicated alcohol withdrawal syndrome and may be useful in identifying individuals who can be managed in the outpatient primary care setting.","Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)

ncdimh-tbl-alcohol-withdrawal-sedative,ncdimh,"Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)",table,ncdimh-tbl-alcohol-withdrawal-sedative,1/1,Chapter 13: Psychiatry > Substance Use Disorder > Alcohol Withdrawal Syndrome,316,316,ncdimh:9f766ec207,ncdimh:98080bcf59,ncdimh-0909,ncdimh-0911,265,"### Alcohol withdrawal syndrome: benzodiazepine (lorazepam) dosing, PAWSS and CIWA-Ar/SAWS assessment, outpatient vs inpatient

Alcohol withdrawal starts 4-12 hours after the last drink (anxiety, agitation, tremor, sympathetic activation; severe: seizures and delirium tremens, potentially fatal); symptoms may last up to 5 days. Mild to moderate withdrawal can be managed as an outpatient in primary care with benzodiazepines; severe withdrawal or complicating conditions need inpatient management. Use the PAWSS to predict severe withdrawal (score <4 = low risk, suitable for outpatient care).

ncdimh-0915,ncdimh,"Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)",text,,,Chapter 13: Psychiatry > Substance Use Disorder > Treatment Targets,319,319,ncdimh:ac1ff2aa40,ncdimh:98080bcf59,ncdimh-tbl-alcohol-dependence-drugs-p3,ncdimh-0916,312,"# Treatment Targets (3)

Long-term cessation of alcohol use is the main treatment goal for alcohol use disorder (AUD). This goal may often be unachievable for many individuals. Alternative goals then may be improved overall health and wellbeing for persons with AUD include:
- Reduced alcohol use
- Cessation or a reduction is high-risk behaviours such as driving while under the influence of alcohol or engaging in alcohol- related unsafe sex.
- Remaining engaged in care and follow up to facilitate prevention, and early diagnosis, and management of other comorbid conditions.
- Improved quality of life and other social indicators, e.g., maintaining stable housing, remaining employed, remaining in school, and avoiding imprisonment.
- Improved overall health and wellbeing.

Care for persons with AUD should be individualized. The healthcare provider should discuss openly treatment and care plans with patients and their caregivers reviewing these regularly as they may need adjustments from time to time. Where necessary, treatment may require intensification with adjunctive therapy such as behavioural interventions and other mental health status assessments. Healthcare workers may often need to adjust or titrate treatment doses accordingly.","Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)

## In-Hospital Management of AUD(3)
In-Hospital management of AUD is recommended for:
- Persons presenting with Severe Alcohol withdrawal syndrome
- Persons with a history of long-term heavy alcohol use.
- Acute or chronic comorbidities, including serious mental illness.
- Persons with a history of withdrawal seizures or high risk of delirium tremens.
- Persons with concurrent use of other drugs.","Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)

## ANXIETY DISORDERS
**Definition(s) and Classification of Anxiety Disorders**

Anxiety is a state of tension, fear, worry and apprehension. It is a natural response to perceived threat. Anxiety is associated with hyperactivity of the autonomic nervous system that triggers fight or flight response. Mild and moderate levels of anxiety are normal and improves performance.
There are different types of anxiety disorders:
- Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD)
- Panic Disorder
- Substance/Medication Induced Anxiety Disorder
- Agoraphobia
- Social Anxiety Disorder
- Separation Anxiety Disorder
- Mutism
- Disruptive Mood Dysregulation Disorder
- Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD) is the commonest anxiety disorder in the country.","Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)

ncdimh-0930,ncdimh,"Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)",text,,,Chapter 13: Psychiatry > Suicide > Assessment of Patients with Suicidal Behaviour,324,324,ncdimh:eb58b25e56,ncdimh:d09cabccba,ncdimh-box-suicidal-behaviour-diagnostic-features,ncdimh-0931,272,"## Assessments of Patients with Suicidal Behaviour
- Previous suicidal attempts.
- Look out for signs of poisoning or intoxication, loss of consciousness, bleeding from self-inflicted wounds or extreme lethargy.
- Previous history of self-harm/suicidal thoughts or plans in the past two weeks – one year.

- For a person who is extremely agitated, violent, distressed or lacks communication, inquire if, in the past two weeks to one month, they have had thoughts or plans to self-harm/suicidal ideations, or if in the past year, they have self-harmed.

- Presence of mental, neurological & substance abuse (MNS) conditions, e.g., depression, child & adolescent mental and behavioural disorders, psychoses, disorders due to substance use, epilepsy, and chronic pain.
- Severity of emotional symptoms:
- ✓ Is the person having difficulty carrying out usual work, school, domestic or social activities?
- ✓ Is the person on repeated self-medication for emotional distress or unexplained physical symptoms?
- ✓ Is the person experiencing marked distress or repeated help-seeking behaviour?","Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)

ncdimh-0931,ncdimh,"Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)",text,,,Chapter 13: Psychiatry > Suicide > Differential Diagnosis and Management of Suicide,324,325,ncdimh:fa1df8c83a,ncdimh:d09cabccba,ncdimh-0930,ncdimh-0933,234,"## **Differential diagnosis**
Self-harming behaviour.
## Management of Suicide
- Assess the physical condition of the patient to ensure that the patient is medically stable by stabilizing the vital signs and appropriately managing any emergencies.
- When medically stable, calm the patient to do a risk assessment.
- Evaluate for underlying psychiatric illness by taking history and mental status examinations.
- A multidisciplinary approach including the role of physicians in medical management of injuries
- **It is best to admit the patient for at least 24 hours with strict vigilance to prevent another suicidal attempt or completion.**
- Remove all potentially harmful objects or means near the patient.
- All medication given should be supervised.

ncdimh-0933,ncdimh,"Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)",text,,,Chapter 13: Psychiatry > Suicide > Psychosocial Management,325,325,ncdimh:e5cbd26874,ncdimh:d09cabccba,ncdimh-0931,ncdimh-0934,403,"## **Psychosocial Management**
This approach can be dual-focused, addressing both the individual and the available caregivers.

Ensure the person is placed within a secure and nurturing environment at a healthcare facility (avoid leaving them unattended). Additionally, take measures to eliminate access to potential means of self- harm.

If the person must wait for treatment, offer an environment that minimizes distress; if possible, in a separate, quiet room with constant supervision and contact with a designated staff or family member to always ensure safety.
Consult a mental health specialist, if available.
**Offer psychoeducation.** Some key messages to the person and the caregivers can include:
- If one has thoughts of suicide, seek help immediately from a trusted family member, friend or health care provider.
- It is okay to talk about suicide. Talking about suicide does not provoke the act of suicide.
- Suicides are preventable.

- Having a suicidal episode is an indicator of severe emotional distress. The person does not see an alternative or a solution. Therefore, getting the person immediate support for emotional problems and stressors is essential.
- Suicidal means (e.g., pesticides, firearms, medications) should be removed from the home.
- Social networks, including the family and significant others, are important for providing social support.
Mobilize active engagement of family, friends, and other concerned individuals, along with available community resources, to oversee and provide support to the individual throughout imminent risk.
Follow the guidelines outlined below:","Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)

- Mobilize family, friends, concerned individuals and other available resources to ensure close monitoring of the person if the risk of suicide persists.

ncdimh-0936,ncdimh,"Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)",text,,,"Chapter 13: Psychiatry > Suicide > Referral, Linkages and Follow-Up",326,326,ncdimh:7eccfedc76,ncdimh:d09cabccba,ncdimh-0935,ncdimh-0937,156,"## Referral & Linkages, and Follow-Up
It is important to follow up on the patient.

**The healthcare worker should maintain regular contact (via telephone and home visits). This will initially be frequent (e.g., daily, weekly) for the first two months.** This should continue for as long as the risk of suicide persists and decreases as the person improves.
If the person does not show signs of improvement, they should be referred to a specialist for further management as required.

**At each point of contact during follow-up, the healthcare worker should regularly assess for thoughts and plans for self-harm/suicide.**","Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)

column1: Diagnostic tests for asthma: spirometry, peak flow, allergy tests, chest X-ray, FeNO, blood tests: utility and interpretation; GINA 2024 positive criteria for variable airflow limitation (part 1 of 2).

Spirometry: Utility & Recommendation: Primary tool to document variable airflow limitation. Recommended for children >6 years; Key Diagnostic Criteria / Interpretation: 1. Baseline: FEV1/FVC ratio <80%. 2. Reversibility: FEV1 increases by >12% (or ≥200 mL) post-bronchodilator.

Peak Flowmetry: Utility & Recommendation: Not for diagnosis (low sensitivity). Good for monitoring exacerbations, especially in 'under-perceivers'; Key Diagnostic Criteria / Interpretation: Children: average daily diurnal PEF variability >12% suggests asthma. Compare the current value to personal best PEF.

Allergy Tests: Utility & Recommendation: Not routinely recommended. Use only for difficult-to-control asthma, allergic rhinitis, or food allergy; Key Diagnostic Criteria / Interpretation: A positive result (skin prick or sIgE) DOES NOT prove causation; must be confirmed by the patient's history.

Chest X-ray: Utility & Recommendation: NOT ROUTINE FOR DIAGNOSIS. Use to rule out alternative conditions (asthma mimics); Key Diagnostic Criteria / Interpretation: May show hyperinflation, atelectasis, or be normal.
FeNO: Utility & Recommendation: Not established for ruling in or ruling out the diagnosis (GINA 2021); Key Diagnostic Criteria / Interpretation: Modestly associated with eosinophil levels.
Blood Tests: Utility & Recommendation: Serum total IgE is NOT useful for diagnosis; Key Diagnostic Criteria / Interpretation: Complete blood count (CBC) may show eosinophilia in atopy."

Diagnosing asthma in under-5s: spirometry is unreliable, so diagnosis is clinical and based on symptom patterns. A therapeutic trial of low-dose ICS (4–8 weeks) is recommended to confirm the diagnosis. Recurrent wheezing (≥3 episodes) in a child with atopy or family history strongly supports asthma. Differential diagnoses include bronchiolitis, viral-induced wheeze, foreign body, tracheomalacia. Reassess the diagnosis regularly, as symptoms may resolve with age.

column1: Asthma drug classes: SABA, ICS, LABA, LTRA, methylxanthines: examples, key points and precautions.

Short-Acting Beta Agonists (SABA): Examples: Salbutamol; Key Points: Mainstay of quick relief; used for acute symptom relief; frequent use suggests poor control; Notes/Precautions: Not for long-term control.

Inhaled Corticosteroids (ICS): Examples: Beclomethasone, budesonide, fluticasone; Key Points: Cornerstone of long-term treatment; safe and effective; use a spacer to improve delivery and reduce oral candidiasis; Notes/Precautions: Dose depends on severity, potency & response; increase ICS if SABA use is frequent.

Leukotriene Receptor Antagonists (LTRA): Examples: Montelukast 10 mg; Key Points: Controls mild persistent asthma; useful in aspirin-induced, exercise-induced, and allergic rhinitis-associated asthma; Notes/Precautions: Less potent than ICS; stop if no benefit within 1 month.

Methylxanthines (second-line): Examples: Theophylline; Key Points: Mild bronchodilator; add-on for persistent asthma; Notes/Precautions: Narrow therapeutic window; requires serum level monitoring (5–15 μg/ml); starting dose 10 mg/kg/day."

ncdimh-box-acute-asthma-immediate,ncdimh,"Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)",text,ncdimh-box-acute-asthma-immediate,1/1,Chapter 14: Pulmonology > Management of Acute Asthma Exacerbations > All Age Groups – Immediate Actions and Admission Criteria,337,337,ncdimh:9202552f97,ncdimh:ce63cba17a,ncdimh-tbl-asthma-long-term-older-format-p2,ncdimh-fig-acute-asthma-primary-care-p1,266,"> **Acute asthma exacerbation: immediate actions for all ages (oxygen, salbutamol, ipratropium, steroids, magnesium) and admission criteria**
> All age groups – immediate actions:
> - Oxygen to achieve SpO2 94–98% (adults/adolescents) or 94–98% (children).
> - SABA: salbutamol 4–10 puffs via MDI + spacer every 20 min × 3 (first hour).
> - Severe: nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg (children) / 5 mg (adults) every 20 min.
> - Ipratropium bromide: add 0.5 mg (adults) / 0.25 mg (children) to the nebuliser for moderate–severe exacerbations.
> - Systemic corticosteroids: prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day (max 40 mg, children) OR 40–50 mg/day (adults) × 5–7 days.
> - IV magnesium sulfate: 2 g IV over 20 min (adults/adolescents) or 25–75 mg/kg (children) for severe exacerbations, SpO2 <92%.

> Admission criteria – refer/admit if ANY: severe or life-threatening features; SpO2 <92% after initial treatment; no improvement after 1 hour of treatment; PEF remains <40% after initial treatment; unable to maintain oral intake (children); concern about home environment/adherence.","Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)

column1: Acute asthma exacerbation: immediate actions for all ages (oxygen, salbutamol, ipratropium, steroids, magnesium) and admission criteria.
All age groups – immediate actions:
- Oxygen to achieve SpO2 94–98% (adults/adolescents) or 94–98% (children).
- SABA: salbutamol 4–10 puffs via MDI + spacer every 20 min × 3 (first hour).
- Severe: nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg (children) / 5 mg (adults) every 20 min.
- Ipratropium bromide: add 0.5 mg (adults) / 0.25 mg (children) to the nebuliser for moderate–severe exacerbations.
- Systemic corticosteroids: prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day (max 40 mg, children) OR 40–50 mg/day (adults) × 5–7 days.
- IV magnesium sulfate: 2 g IV over 20 min (adults/adolescents) or 25–75 mg/kg (children) for severe exacerbations, SpO2 <92%.

Admission criteria – refer/admit if ANY: severe or life-threatening features; SpO2 <92% after initial treatment; no improvement after 1 hour of treatment; PEF remains <40% after initial treatment; unable to maintain oral intake (children); concern about home environment/adherence."

ncdimh-fig-acute-asthma-primary-care-p1,ncdimh,"Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)",diagram,ncdimh-fig-acute-asthma-primary-care,1/2,Chapter 14: Pulmonology > Management of Acute Asthma Exacerbations > Management of acute asthma in primary care,338,338,ncdimh:4f11f04158,ncdimh:ce63cba17a,ncdimh-box-acute-asthma-immediate,ncdimh-fig-acute-asthma-hospital-p1,479,"### Acute or sub-acute asthma exacerbation in primary care (flowchart): assessment, severity (mild/moderate, severe, life-threatening), treatment, transfer, discharge and follow-up
1. Patient presents with an acute or sub-acute asthma exacerbation. Assess: is it asthma? Risk factors for asthma-related death? Severity of the exacerbation?
2. Severity:

- Mild or moderate: talks in phrases; prefers sitting to lying; not agitated; respiratory rate increased; accessory muscles used; pulse 100-120 bpm; O2 saturation (on air) 90-95%; PEF >50% predicted or best (printed '50%').
- Severe: talks in words; sits hunched; agitated; respiratory rate >30/min; accessory muscles used; pulse >120/min; O2 saturation (on air) <90%; PEF <50% predicted or best.
- Life-threatening: drowsy; confused; silent chest.

3. Mild/moderate: start treatment: SABA 4-10 puffs by pMDI + spacer, repeat every 20 min for 1 hour; prednisolone adults 40-50 mg, children 1-2 mg/kg (max 40 mg); controlled oxygen (if available), target saturation 93-95% (children 94-98%).
- Worsening → transfer to an acute care facility.
- Improving → continue SABA as needed; assess response at 1 hour (or earlier).
4. Severe or life-threatening → transfer to an acute care facility; while waiting give SABA, ipratropium bromide, oxygen, systemic corticosteroids.
5. Assess for discharge: symptoms improved, SABA not needed; PEF improving and >60-80% of personal best or predicted; oxygen saturation >94% on room air; adequate resources at home.

6. Follow-up: review symptoms and signs (is the exacerbation resolving? should prednisolone be continued?). Reliever: reduce to as needed. Controller: continue a higher dose short term (1-2 weeks) or long term (3 months) depending on the background to the exacerbation. Risk factors: check and correct modifiable risk factors, including inhaler technique and adherence; refer if >1-2 exacerbations.","Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)

ncdimh-fig-acute-asthma-primary-care-p2,ncdimh,"Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)",diagram,ncdimh-fig-acute-asthma-primary-care,2/2,Chapter 14: Pulmonology > Management of Acute Asthma Exacerbations > Management of acute asthma in primary care,338,338,ncdimh:4f11f04158,ncdimh:ce63cba17a,ncdimh-box-acute-asthma-immediate,ncdimh-fig-acute-asthma-hospital-p1,479,"### Acute or sub-acute asthma exacerbation in primary care (flowchart): assessment, severity (mild/moderate, severe, life-threatening), treatment, transfer, discharge and follow-up

2. Severity:

- Mild or moderate: talks in phrases; prefers sitting to lying; not agitated; respiratory rate increased; accessory muscles used; pulse 100-120 bpm; O2 saturation (on air) 90-95%; PEF >50% predicted or best (printed '50%').
- Severe: talks in words; sits hunched; agitated; respiratory rate >30/min; accessory muscles used; pulse >120/min; O2 saturation (on air) <90%; PEF <50% predicted or best.
- Life-threatening: drowsy; confused; silent chest.

3. Mild/moderate: start treatment: SABA 4-10 puffs by pMDI + spacer, repeat every 20 min for 1 hour; prednisolone adults 40-50 mg, children 1-2 mg/kg (max 40 mg); controlled oxygen (if available), target saturation 93-95% (children 94-98%).
- Worsening → transfer to an acute care facility.
- Improving → continue SABA as needed; assess response at 1 hour (or earlier).
4. Severe or life-threatening → transfer to an acute care facility; while waiting give SABA, ipratropium bromide, oxygen, systemic corticosteroids.
5. Assess for discharge: symptoms improved, SABA not needed; PEF improving and >60-80% of personal best or predicted; oxygen saturation >94% on room air; adequate resources at home.

6. Follow-up: review symptoms and signs (is the exacerbation resolving? should prednisolone be continued?). Reliever: reduce to as needed. Controller: continue a higher dose short term (1-2 weeks) or long term (3 months) depending on the background to the exacerbation. 1. Initial assessment: A airway, B breathing, C circulation. Any of drowsiness, confusion, silent chest? → consult ICU, start SABA and O2, and prepare the patient for intubation.
2. Further triage by clinical status, according to the worst feature:

- Mild or moderate: talks in phrases; prefers sitting to lying down; not agitated; respiratory rate increased; accessory muscles not used; pulse rate 100-120 bpm (printed '100-200'); O2 saturation (on air) 90-95%; PEF >50% predicted or best. Treat: short-acting beta agonists; O2 to maintain saturation 94-98%; oral corticosteroids.

- Severe: talks in words; sits hunched forwards; agitated; respiratory rate >30/min; accessory muscles being used; pulse rate >120 bpm; O2 saturation (on air) <90%; PEF <50% predicted or best. Treat: short-acting beta2 agonists; ipratropium bromide; O2 to maintain saturation 94-98%; oral or IV corticosteroids; consider IV magnesium sulfate; IV terbutaline/IV aminophylline.
- If continuing deterioration, treat as severe and reassess for ICU; transfer if necessary.
3. Assess clinical progress frequently; measure lung function in all patients one hour after initial treatment:
- FEV1 or PEF 60-80% of predicted or personal best and symptoms improved (moderate): consider discharge.
- FEV1 or PEF <60% of predicted or personal best, or lack of clinical response (severe): continue treatment as above and reassess frequently.

IV salbutamol can be used in severe asthma failing other treatments, mainly to prevent intubation; evidence that IV beta2-agonists shorten recovery or improve lung function is very limited. Inhaled drugs may have limited effect with near-complete obstruction and in ventilated patients. Side effects: arrhythmia, tachycardia, raised lactate and anxiety (may increase respiratory workload). Patients on IV salbutamol should be in an ICU setting.

Most guidelines do not recommend IV aminophylline (low efficacy and safety). If used, reserve it for severe exacerbations failing maximal therapy (continuous inhaled beta2-agonists, IV corticosteroids, IV magnesium sulfate), generally in high care/ICU. Its risk-benefit balance is unfavourable.","Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)

ncdimh-fig-copd-stepwise,ncdimh,"Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)",diagram,ncdimh-fig-copd-stepwise,1/1,Chapter 14: Pulmonology > Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease > Step-Wise Management for COPD: Pharmacological Interventions,344,344,ncdimh:1b79d7068e,ncdimh:2e4ab3031e,ncdimh-tbl-copd-severity,ncdimh-0986,354,"### Stepwise pharmacological management of COPD: short-acting bronchodilators, combinations, long-acting bronchodilator, ICS, theophylline; asthma-COPD overlap
Non-pharmacological: smoking cessation and/or nicotine replacement therapy.
1. Start a short-acting bronchodilator for relief of breathlessness: beta2 agonist, e.g. salbutamol 100-200 mcg (1-2 puffs) as needed, OR anticholinergic, e.g. ipratropium 20-40 mcg 3-4 times a day.
2. Poor symptom control → combine short-acting bronchodilators from different groups, e.g. salbutamol and ipratropium (as above).
3. Poor symptom control → consider adding a long-acting bronchodilator (beta2 agonist or anticholinergic), e.g. salmeterol 50 mcg BD, with short-acting bronchodilator(s) as above.

column1: Management of gross haematuria by pathway: haemodynamically unstable, stable with clot retention, stable without clot retention.

Signs to look out for: Pathway 1: Hemodynamically Unstable: Hypotension, tachycardia, active bleeding; Pathway 2: Stable + Clot Retention: Suprapubic pain, bladder distension, inability to void; Pathway 3: Stable, No Clot Retention: Visible hematuria, able to void.

Initial priority: Pathway 1: Hemodynamically Unstable: Resuscitation; Pathway 2: Stable + Clot Retention: Relieve obstruction; Pathway 3: Stable, No Clot Retention: Investigate cause. Send urine for M/C/S. If terminal hematuria, send a specimen between 10am and 2pm to look for schistosomiasis and treat accordingly.

Immediate actions: Pathway 1: Hemodynamically Unstable: ATLS protocol; IV fluids ± blood; Pathway 2: Stable + Clot Retention: 3-way catheter; manual washout; Pathway 3: Stable, No Clot Retention: Basic investigations.
Bladder management: Pathway 1: Hemodynamically Unstable / Pathway 2: Stable + Clot Retention: 3-way catheter + continuous irrigation; Pathway 3: Stable, No Clot Retention: Not routinely required.
Investigations: Pathway 1: Hemodynamically Unstable: After stabilisation; Pathway 2: Stable + Clot Retention: After decompression; Pathway 3: Stable, No Clot Retention: UA, U&E, ultrasound.

Disposition: Pathway 1: Hemodynamically Unstable: Urgent urology referral; Pathway 2: Stable + Clot Retention: Urology referral; Pathway 3: Stable, No Clot Retention: All gross hematuria → urology referral.
ALL CLIENTS PRESENTING WITH GROSS HEMATURIA SHOULD BE REFERRED TO THE UROLOGIST."

ncdimh-fig-microhematuria,ncdimh,"Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)",diagram,ncdimh-fig-microhematuria,1/1,Chapter 15: Urology > Hematuria > Management of Microhematuria,349,349,ncdimh:64e9586855,ncdimh:bb5364acd1,ncdimh-tbl-gross-hematuria-pathways,ncdimh-tbl-aua-microhematuria-risk,388,"### Management of microscopic haematuria (flowchart): confirm, infection, glomerular cause, other causes, imaging, cytology, cystoscopy, follow-up
1. Microscopic evaluation to confirm RBCs (>3 RBC/HPF) in 2 of 3 samples.
2. Signs or symptoms of infection (dysuria, frequency, flank pain, leukocyte esterase, nitrites, white cells, bacteria)?
- Yes: treat the infection; confirm resolution of microscopic haematuria with a follow-up urinalysis 6 weeks after completing therapy.

3. Findings supporting a glomerular cause (proteinuria, elevated creatinine, red cell casts, dysmorphic RBCs, abnormal sediment, ≥5-10 WBC/HPF, or reduced renal function)? Yes: refer to a nephrologist. (Cytology is a poor screening test and is not recommended in the initial workup.)
4. No: other aetiology probable (vigorous exercise, urethral trauma, menstruation, offending medication)? Yes: retest urine after the possible contributing factor is stopped.
5. No: radiographic evaluation of the urinary tract (renal ultrasonography, CT, or IVP, considering availability and costs). If imaging is not available, refer to a urologist.
- If imaging is positive: refer to a urology subspecialist. If negative: urine cytology.
- Negative findings and low risk (age <40 and no risk factors): follow-up with urinalysis and blood pressure; if haematuria persists >3 months, consider specialist referral.

- Positive findings, or all patients >40, or younger patients with risk factors for urothelial tumours: refer to a urology subspecialist for cystoscopy.","Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)

## **Erectile Function Disorders**

This is a spectrum of disorders ranging from Erectile Dysfunction (ED) to Persistent Ejaculations (PE), ED and anejaculation or anorgasmia. ED and PE are mostly seen especially amongst individuals with NCDs. It is therefore important not to neglect penile complications as part of target organ damage in patients with DM/hypertension/metabolic syndrome.

ncdimh-fig-ed-primary-care,ncdimh,"Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)",diagram,ncdimh-fig-ed-primary-care,1/1,Chapter 15: Urology > Erectile Function Disorders > Guidelines for Primary Care Management of Erectile Dysfunction,354,354,ncdimh:776f673eae,ncdimh:6f6eb48b1d,ncdimh-1009,ncdimh-tbl-pde5-comparison,367,"### Primary care management of erectile dysfunction (flowchart): initial assessment, psychogenic vs organic features, investigations, hypogonadism, PDE5 inhibitors, CHD, referral

1. GP initial assessment: sexual history, relevant blood tests, blood pressure, genital examination. ALL young patients with a history of trauma and/or penile/testicular abnormalities on clinical examination SHOULD BE REFERRED TO UROLOGY IMMEDIATELY.

2a. Suggests psychogenic: sudden onset; good or better early-morning / self-stimulated erections; relationship problems; variable depending on circumstances → first-line treatment with PDE5 inhibitors and monitor response; consider counselling.

2b. Suggests organic: gradual onset; lack of tumescence; normal libido; relevant medical history; smoker; difficulty with penetration → further investigations: BMI, BP, abdominal circumference, HbA1c, lipogram; encourage weight loss.
3. Clinical features suggestive of hypogonadism: testosterone (before 10 am) and thyroid function; if testosterone low, do FSH, LH, prolactin, SHBG.
- If abnormal: refer to urology / endocrinology as appropriate.
- If normal with no evidence of CHD: first-line treatment with PDE5 inhibitors.
- Normal but with CHD: guidance from cardiology/medicine; once the patient is low risk according to Princeton criteria, consider PDE5 inhibitors.

PDE5 inhibitors: sildenafil (Viagra); tadalafil (Cialis) – consider daily dose if possible; vardenafil (Levitra).","Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH)

# **1 INTRODUCTION**
# 1.1 Background

The 2022 Eswatini Integrated HIV Management Guidelines are aligned with the National Health Sector HIV/AIDS Response Plan and current global guidance including the WHO's Consolidated Guidelines on HIV Prevention, Testing, Treatment, Service Delivery and Monitoring: Recommendations For a Public Health Approach (July 2021). These Guidelines replace the 2018 Integrated HIV Management Guidelines.

The Eswatini National AIDS Program (SNAP) thematic leads led the development of these guidelines, providing leadership, coordination, and critical reviews. Sub-Technical working groups, such as HTS, LCM, Prevention, Adult care and treatment, Adherence and psychological care and support, non-communicable diseases, STIs, TB/HIV and Advanced HIV, PMTCT and Paediatric Care and Treatment created specialized content for each chapter. Experts from the Ministry of Health, bilateral, multilateral, and implementing partner organizations drafted the respective sections of the guidelines. Additional input was received from WHO and other international experts.

These guidelines aim to standardize and promote the continued provision of comprehensive, quality, and client-centred prevention, care and treatment services. The goal of these new guidelines is to promote service uptake and retention, resulting in improved client outcomes, improved quality of life, and a decline in new HIV infections, HIV-related illnesses and mortality. After surpassing the 2020 UNAIDS targets, the country's goal is to sustain the successes achieved so far while offering patient-centred care."

• Management of Hypertension in a client with HIV follows similar treatment protocols as for HIV-negative clients. However:
○ Calcium channel inhibitors should be used with caution as they may interact with PIs producing increased serum levels of the former. Therefore, dose titration and ECG monitoring are required.

Medical male circumcision should be offered to all men/boys 10 years and older, especially those who are HIV-negative.
### *Early infant male circumcision*

Early infant male circumcision (EIMC) is promoted during antenatal care (ANC) and is offered in labour and post-delivery. Preferably, EIMC should occur within the first 60 days of life (8 weeks). hiv-2022-0050,hiv-2022,Eswatini Integrated HIV Management Guidelines (2022),text,,,2 HIV Prevention > Voluntary medical male circumcision,34,34,hiv-2022:4a9a7470f5,hiv-2022:6858840d21,hiv-2022-0049,hiv-2022-0051,315,"# *Voluntary medical male circumcision*

Voluntary medical male circumcision (VMMC) in Eswatini is provided by trained HCWs at health facilities or during outreach programs to adolescent and adult males. The surgical and device-based procedure can be performed by trained nurses or doctors following adequate IPC measures including proper disinfection and sterilisation procedures for reusable equipment. For male circumcision for HIV prevention, Eswatini only allows the use of the dorsal slit method for all surgical and Shang Ring for device-based procedures. Priority groups include men/boys aged 10–49 and all sexually active men. While the conduct of MCs to males aged 15 years and older is recommended in other settings, the national program desires to provide VMMC services to adolescents between the age of 10- and 14 years using a device-based method while maintaining the safety of the procedure and paying attention to the boys' capacity to provide informed consent.

To mitigate serious Adverse Events (AE) amongst adolescents with immature genitalia health care workers are encouraged to take note and evaluate the physical maturity of under 15 adolescent boys and defer the service until the penis is mature or offer a device-based circumcision.","Eswatini Integrated HIV Management Guidelines (2022)

ARV drugs used for oral PrEP do not have any known interactions with contraceptive hormones and do not affect levels of gender-affirming hormones used by transgender individuals. There is some indication that the use of oestradiol-based exogenous hormones may reduce oral PrEP drug levels in people assigned male at birth (AMAB). Males may switch between ED-PrEP and daily PrEP due to changes in relationship status or sex partner(s) or moving to a new location, whereby the frequency and predictability of sex changes, or when a client's preferred dosing option changes. The ring is made of a flexible silicone material containing 25mg of a slow-released Non-Nucleoside Reverse Transcriptase Inhibitor (NNRTI) called Dapivirine. ### 2.6 Post-Exposure Prophylaxis
* Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) is the use of ARVs by HIV-negative people after the potential exposure to HIV to prevent infection with HIV.
* All persons potentially exposed to HIV accidentally, occupationally, sexually or otherwise should access PEP as early as 1 hour and within 72 hours to minimise the risk of transmission of HIV.

* All Registered doctors and nurses at any health facility level or community service delivery point can prescribe ARV drugs for PEP for any individual who presents with a history of exposure to HIV in the past 72 hours.
* A three-drug regimen is preferred for PEP."

column3:
- HIV PEP should be offered and initiated as early as possible for all individuals with the exposure that has the potential for HIV transmission, within 72 hours.
- Eligibility assessment should be based on the HIV status of the source of potential exposure whenever possible and may include consideration of background prevalence and local epidemiological patterns.
- The following types of exposure may warrant PEP: - ○ Body fluids: blood, blood-stained saliva, breast milk, genital secretions, cerebrospinal, amniotic, peritoneal, synovial, pericardial, or pleural fluids. - ○ Types of exposure: Mucous membrane from sexual exposure, splashes to the eye, nose or oral cavity and parenteral exposures. - ○ All clients should be assessed, and PEP should be offered to any client with any of the exposures as indicated above. - The exposure that does not require PEP includes: - ○ When the exposed individual is already HIV positive - ○ When the source of potential exposure is established to be HIV-negative unless the source has had an HIV exposure in the last 14 days and could be in the window period. - ○ Exposure to body fluids that do not pose a significant risk: tears, non-blood-stained saliva, urine and sweat.

column1: ## **2.6.1 ART for People living with HIV**

ARV drugs play a key role in HIV prevention. Treating PLHIV with ART is one of the effective strategies for preventing new HIV infections as PLHIV who achieve and maintain an undetectable viral load-the amount of HIV in the blood—by taking ART daily as prescribed cannot sexually transmit the virus to others. All people living with HIV are eligible to start ART regardless of CD4 count or WHO staging and HCWs should promote early ART initiation."

When the viral load falls below 200 copies/ml, the protective effect of ART for preventing new infections approaches 100%.
People taking ARVs who **achieve and maintain** undetectable viral load have close to zero chances of transmitting HIV to their sexual partners.

hiv-2022-0119,hiv-2022,Eswatini Integrated HIV Management Guidelines (2022),text,,,3 HIV Testing Services > 3.2 HIV testing service delivery approaches > 3.2.3 Partner Notification Services/ Index testing services,55,55,hiv-2022:dd2d40d715,hiv-2022:ec27f523fd,hiv-2022-0118,hiv-2022-0120,201,"# 3.2.3 **Partner Notification Services/ Index testing services**
Partner notification and index testing services include:
- partner notification
- contact tracing
- index contact testing and family-based index case testing
- social network–based approaches.

All partner notification services should be voluntary. Whenever partner notification services and social network–based approaches are offered, the client should be informed of their benefits and potential risks and assured that their decisions about contacting partners and other people from their social networks are voluntary and not pressured. All index testing services must adhere to WHO's 5Cs minimum standards (consent, counselling, confidentiality, correct test results, and connection to appropriate HIV prevention and treatment services","Eswatini Integrated HIV Management Guidelines (2022)

hiv-2022-0120,hiv-2022,Eswatini Integrated HIV Management Guidelines (2022),text,,,3 HIV Testing Services > 3.2 HIV testing service delivery approaches > 3.2.3 Partner Notification Services/ Index testing services > Partner notification approaches (methods),55,55,hiv-2022:46c4d34df9,hiv-2022:dd2d40d715,hiv-2022-0119,hiv-2022-0121,416,"## Partner notification approaches (methods)
1. *Passive partner notification methods:*

Passive referral or client referral refers to when HIV-positive clients are encouraged by a trained provider to disclose their status to their sexual and drug injecting partners by themselves and to also suggest HIV testing to the partner(s), given their potential exposure to HIV infection.
2. *Assisted partner notification methods:*

**I.Provider:** Using the opt-out approach, a trained provider agrees with the HIV-positive client that they (the Health provider) will confidentially contact the HIV-positive client's partner(s) directly and offer the partner voluntary HTS.
<mark>Provider-assisted partner notification is the preferred method and should be prioritized.</mark>

**II.Contract:** When an HIV-positive client enters a contract with a trained provider to refer their partners to HTS within an agreed period (14 days) after which the provider contacts the partners (with the client's permission) directly and offers voluntary HTS.
**III.Dual:** When a trained provider accompanies an HIV-positive client when they disclose their HIV status to their partner(s). The provider also offers voluntary HTS to the partners.
**IV.Client referral:** when a trained provider requests the client to disclose their HIV status to their partner(s).

Care is needed to ensure the correct person is receiving the message, and that the anonymity/confidentiality of both the HIV-positive client and the notified partner is maintained. Couples and partners should be offered voluntary HTS with support for mutual disclosure to their possible contacts that may also have HIV.","Eswatini Integrated HIV Management Guidelines (2022)

hiv-2022-0125,hiv-2022,Eswatini Integrated HIV Management Guidelines (2022),text,,,3 HIV Testing Services > 3.3 Intimate partner violence screening tool > IPV screening tool,57,57,hiv-2022:950c0de21e,hiv-2022:03fa5178a1,hiv-2022-0124,hiv-2022-0127,485,"## IPV screening tool
**SCREEN FOR PROBABLE INDEX TESTING INDUCED HEALTH RISK**
NB: Ask the question below for each of the partners listed
Do you anticipate any violence with partner (current or former) if/ when you disclose your HIV results??""
Yes <mark> </mark> No <mark> </mark>
If patient answer ""NO"" to the above question:
1. Record the patient as ""Not at risk"" in the index testing register
2. DO NOT offer provider referral
3. You can offer Client referral, Contract referral and Dual referral depending on the patient preference.
If patient answer ""YES"" to the above question:
Record the patient as ""at risk"" in the index testing register

For all patients answering ""YES"" the counsellor is requested to ask the patients to share his/her limitations about possible violence from the partner or partners (current/ former) using the prompts below.
Then depending on the nature of the limitations advise on the most appropriate disclosure strategy such as the use of Provider Referral.

1. **Do you think your partner (current/ former) will physically hurt you or force you to do something sexually that makes you feel uncomfortable if you disclose to him/her or he/she finds out your HIV status?**
2. **Do you think your partner (current/ former) will emotionally hurt you if you disclose to him/her your HIV status or he/she finds out your HIV status?**
3. **Do you fear your partner (current/ former) will abandon you or chase you from the place you live or stop paying/ contributing towards rent/ bond?**
4. **Do you think your partner (current/ former) will stop financially supporting you or your children?**

**NOTE: If client appears agitated, sweaty, restless, crying or irritable during the discussion, stop all questions and refer to <u>Health Provider</u> for further <u>counseling management</u> (<u>debriefing</u> / <u>Psychological First Aid</u> / <u>Cognitive Behavior Therapy</u> / <u>Clinical Therapy</u>)</u>**","Eswatini Integrated HIV Management Guidelines (2022)

HIV Rapid diagnostic tests detect antibodies to HIV and can be used to definitively diagnose adults and children 18 months of age or older. Eswatini has adopted the *two-test strategy* for the diagnosis of HIV. The two rapid tests approved for use are - **Determine** HIV1/2 and **UniGold** HIV1/2. However, a three-test strategy should be considered if HIV positivity in HIV testing services falls below 5%. *Also in ANC settings, the **dual HIV/Syphilis** rapid diagnostic tests may be considered the first test in the HIV testing strategy and algorithms.*
The **Asante** HIV-1 Rapid Recency assay is used to detect recent infection (an infection that was acquired within the past 12 months) among all newly diagnosed individuals 15 years and above.

The **Ora-Quick** HIV self-test is a triage test and does not provide a definitive HIV-positive diagnosis. A reactive (positive) HIV self-testing result needs to be followed by further testing from a trained provider to confirm HIV status, following the national testing algorithm.","Eswatini Integrated HIV Management Guidelines (2022)

- Nucleic acid testing (NAT) technologies for the qualitative detection of HIV DNA and/or RNA in whole-blood, plasma or dried blood spot can be used to definitively diagnose children less than 18 months of age. Serological antibody assays are not suitable for diagnosis since trans-placentially transmitted maternal HIV antibodies may persist in the child up until 18 months of age.
- The use of point-of-care technologies and the addition of NAT at birth (0-3 days) can improve rapid identification and treatment initiation among exposed infants.
- NAT (RNA and/or DNA PCR) may also be used to provide a definite diagnosis in case of a discordant result following HIV re-testing for verification before ART initiation.

- NAT (RNA and/or DNA PCR) may also be used as the last step to provide a definite diagnosis in case of an inconclusive test result in adults and children above 18 months.","Eswatini Integrated HIV Management Guidelines (2022)

A summary of the HIV testing algorithm for infants from birth is in *Figure 3.8* below
**Flowchart: HIV testing algorithm for infants and children**"

However, several factors should be considered when assessing infants for ART interruption after discordant test results (positive then a negative result) are followed by a third test with a negative result:
* The infant ought to have no clinical signs or symptoms suggesting HIV infection;
* A follow-up plan should be agreed on with the family, caregiver(s) and healthcare staff; and
* Tracking information (phone, address, etc.) of the family and caregiver(s) should be collected and confirmed.
The following factors should be considered when following up on any infant undergoing treatment interruption.
- Active follow-up is needed to ensure that a potentially infected infant is retained in care and reinitiates treatment if a viral rebound occurs.
- Viral rebound among infants living with HIV starting treatment early is expected to happen within eight months of interruption in >99% of cases).
- Infants who develop signs and symptoms indicating HIV infection should undergo immediate testing.
- Breastfeeding and continued risk of transmission require follow-up and appropriate testing throughout risk until final diagnosis.

- There is value in minimizing follow-up testing by leveraging existing opportunities for infant testing (based on the national infant testing schedule and immunization or well-child appointment schedules) until a final diagnosis is ascertained.

column2: 1. Perform testing with Test 1 (Determine) through a finger-prick.
2. If non-reactive, the result is interpreted and communicated as HIV-negative.
3. If reactive, a second test is done using Test 2 (UniGold).
4. If Test 2 (UniGold) is reactive, the result is interpreted and communicated as HIV-positive.

5. If Test 2 (UniGold) is non-reactive (i.e., Determine and UniGold are inconclusive), repeat testing using Test 1 (Determine) and Test 2 (UniGold) in parallel. Collecting blood by venepuncture is recommended to minimize client discomfort from subsequent multiple finger pricks.
6. If both repeat tests are non-reactive, the result is interpreted and communicated as HIV-negative.
7. If both repeat tests are reactive, the result is interpreted and communicated as HIV-positive.
8. If repeat tests remain Inconclusive (i.e., Determine test is reactive and UniGold test is non-reactive, or vice versa), appoint the client in two weeks and repeat parallel testing.
9. If both repeat tests are non-reactive, the result is interpreted and communicated as HIV-negative.
10. If both repeat tests are reactive, the result is interpreted and communicated as HIV-positive.

hiv-2022-0170,hiv-2022,Eswatini Integrated HIV Management Guidelines (2022),text,,,3 HIV Testing Services > 3.11 Testing for Recent Infection > Laboratory Testing Methods > Interpretation of RTRI Results,72,72,hiv-2022:12a7d79c64,hiv-2022:18f6ae14a1,hiv-2022-0169,hiv-2022-0171,332,"### Interpretation of RTRI Results

The HIV status of the client will be determined as outlined in the national HIV testing algorithm using a two-test process. The result of the RTRI will not impact the client’s HIV diagnosis or clinical management and will only be used to determine recency status for surveillance purposes. RTRI results should be interpreted as follows:
* The presence of a control line (C), a verification line (V) and a long-term line (LT) on the RTRI will indicate an RTRI long-term infection.
* The presence of a control line and a verification line will indicate an RTRI recent infection.

* The presence of only a control line on the RTRI will indicate inconclusive RTRI results and will be recorded as HIV positive (if Determine and UniGold were both positive) with inconclusive recency status.
* The absence of a control line on the RTRI will indicate an invalid recency result.
* The presence of a long-term line without a verification line also represents an invalid recency test result.

If Determine is reactive and UniGold is nonreactive, the result of the RTRI will not be reported as the client has not been confirmed to be HIV positive at that point. If the client is later confirmed to be HIV positive, recency testing will be performed according to the recent infection testing algorithm (RITA).","Eswatini Integrated HIV Management Guidelines (2022)

hiv-2022-0171,hiv-2022,Eswatini Integrated HIV Management Guidelines (2022),text,,,3 HIV Testing Services > 3.11 Testing for Recent Infection > Laboratory Testing Methods > Recent Infection Testing Algorithm,72,73,hiv-2022:24024f5f8d,hiv-2022:18f6ae14a1,hiv-2022-0170,hiv-2022-0172,228,"### Recent Infection Testing Algorithm

Clients with a recent infection status on the RTRI will be tested for HIV-1 viral load levels to classify recent infection status according to the RITA. Clients with RTRI recent infection status and a viral load result ≥ 1,000 copies/mL will be categorized as a RITA recent infection (Figure 2). A viral load of fewer than 1,000 copies/mL will be interpreted as a RITA long-term infection.
Clients that test long-term on the RTRI do not require additional testing and are classified as an RTRI long-term infection according to the RITA.

## **4.1 Introduction**
* In Eswatini HIV testing and treatment programs have increased access to ART remarkably, however many PLHIV still initiate ART late, particularly males and people diagnosed in the communities.

* Linkages case management (LCM) is a Ministry of Health initiative, mainly aimed at the implementation of more efficient and effective ways that ensures clients testing HIV-negative are linked to prevention services and those testing HIV positive are linked to chronic HIV care. The client may either be referred from other health facilities or the community (Community ART)

* LCM is a peer-delivered model which includes individualized service, navigation, and index testing. LCM has been extended to 6 months to help improve the retention of clients on ART-enhanced LCM (eLCM)
* Patient-centred care for the different subpopulations must be implemented to improve linkages.
* The following strategies are aimed at improving HIV linkages:
- flexi hours
- integration of ART in all health facility departments
- escorting clients to ART units and HIV prevention services
- provision of comprehensive male and adolescent-friendly services in high-volume facilities
- provision of community ART initiation or HIV prevention services depending on the client’s HIV status
- provision of escalation counselling for clients not ready to be initiated.
* Caregivers of children, and adolescents are to be provided with support for re-engaging to care.
* Rapid ART initiation should be emphasized for all PLHIV following a confirmed HIV diagnosis preferably on the same day of diagnosis (in line with the Test and Start policy)."

## **4.11 Clients returning to care**

Any clients who return to the facility either of their own accord or after tracing, more than 28 days after missing an appointment are said to be returning to care. Clients should be provided with the returning to care package as indicated in the enhanced *LCM SOP* ***enhanced SOP (pages 62-67)***. Clients must be actively followed up in all stages to bring them back to care.
There are different stages of treatment interrupters, which are:
* immediate (<28-day post-initiation)
* early interrupters (>28 days <6 months) and,
* late interrupters (+6 months).
**Flowchart: Stages of HIV care and treatment**","Eswatini Integrated HIV Management Guidelines (2022)

hiv-2022-0202,hiv-2022,Eswatini Integrated HIV Management Guidelines (2022),text,,,5 Basic Care Package for HIV-Positive Individuals > Important Contacts,84,85,hiv-2022:1a0f7171a2,hiv-2022:e478dc99bb,hiv-2022-0201,hiv-2022-0203,416,"## **Important Contacts:**
National Pharmacovigilance Centre
WhatsApp number +268 7655 7303

All clients who test HIV-positive should be linked to and enrolled on HIV chronic care on the same day of diagnosis. All health facilities should provide the basic HIV chronic care package as defined in this chapter.
The basic HIV chronic care package for people living with HIV (PLHIV) includes:
- Initial clinical evaluation and categorization of clients.
- Opportunistic infection screening and management, including the provision of prophylactic
- Adherence and psychosocial support services.
- Patient Education
- HIV index testing.
- Linkage to care and treatment
- Laboratory tests.
- Routine and structured clinical follow-up visits.
- Integration of HIV services with other health services such as
- TB
- Sexual and reproductive health i.e., family planning and cervical cancer screening and management
- HIV prevention services including the provision of condoms and STI screening and management
- Hepatitis B screening and management
- Non-communicable disease screening and management
- Mental health screening and management
- Palliative care
- Nutritional assessment
- Immunisation
The basic HIV chronic care package should be differentiated based on the client's laboratory and clinical evaluation findings. See Table 5.2 for definitions of relevant categories.

Pharmacovigilance is also an integral part of HIV service delivery. All adverse events should be reported to the National pharmacovigilance Centre. These include adverse events from all the medical products a patient on ART patient is taking. See Section 5.12","Eswatini Integrated HIV Management Guidelines (2022)
